The effectiveness of graph neural networks for feature dimension reduction will be explored, specifically in contexts where the dimensions represent multiple components or subspaces. Several graph neural network architectures are introduced, each utilizing a different type of subspace representation. These models are then applied to two high-dimensional data sets: a synthetic dataset and a dataset related to the detection of faults in industrial processes. The performance of these models will be compared to that of traditional subspace learning techniques to assess their effectiveness. Additionally, the impact of varying model parameters on their performance will be examined using techniques of differential analysis. Based on these findings, a new method called Multiple Subspace Graph Neural Network (MS-GNN) will be developed and demonstrated to outperform existing models.

The Sidon set completeness problem, a challenge originating from the finite affine plane, has been reexamined using a hyperbola or ellipse framework. Through this alternative perspective, the sets corresponding to hyperbolas or ellipses have been characterized as being complete if and only if they exclude specific parallel lines or line pairs, which coincidentally aligns with prior descriptions for hyperbolas. Additionally, it has been found that complete Sidon sets formed from hyperbolas or ellipses maintain a consistent pattern in the difference of their x-coordinates, a characteristic unique to these sets.

Researchers are increasingly applying deep learning to analyze binary matrices, a challenge known as binary matrix factorization. To enhance the representational capabilities of neural networks, researchers often use large, randomly sampled binary matrices as inputs. The effectiveness of this approach depends heavily on how the sampling probability is distributed. Our research reveals that non-uniform sampling outperforms uniform sampling by utilizing the statistical properties of the resulting matrices, which are underexplored. By drawing upon the properties of combinatorial central limits, we develop a probabilistic framework that informs binary matrix factorization through normalization. The proposed approach surpasses existing methods in both synthetic and real-world scenarios, according to our experiments.

A unique approach is presented for solving a system of integral equations that describe the behavior of parton distribution functions (PDFs) within the framework of the DGLAP formalism. The method involves using a set of measured PDFs at various scales and linking them through the DGLAP evolution equations. The evolution process is treated as a dynamic system, and a kinetic-like equation is introduced to describe the transition of PDFs between different scales. The solution to this problem is framed as a multistep optimization task. At each step, the PDFs are varied to maximize the agreement between the measured and evolved PDFs at the current scale. The method is applied to fitting PDFs using data from deep-inelastic scattering experiments at different scales, and the results are shown to be in good agreement with existing fitting procedures. The study also explores the potential for using next-to-leading-order DGLAP kernels and evolved PDFs as an initial condition for further refinements using higher-order DGLAP or balanced equations.

This document outlines the concepts and techniques utilized in ELKI, a widely-used data mining framework, and describes its implementation, highlighting its advantages in terms of scalability and performance through optimized efficient data structures and operations.  By offering both command-line and programmable interfaces, ELKI aims to balance ease of use and flexibility to support various data mining tasks.  This document serves as a reference manual for users and developers interested in contributing to the project.

In our experiment, we generate a microcomb with an anomalous dispersion profile, yielding a continuously varying spectrum with changing pump-power-dependent spectral features. By adjusting the pump-laser's frequency, we create sidebands that spacing changes, resulting in a maximum of eight observable sidebands, with as few as three being present at a different pump-laser frequency. As the pump power increases, the microcomb's spectrum undergoes transformation, ultimately becoming a typical, discrete comb spectrum, with the creation of a new, higher-order sideband occurring at a specific increased pump power. With our findings, a pathway is presented for developing optimized, high-performance optical microcombs, with controllable and predictable features.

We establish that for any non-identically distributed sequence of natural numbers, $\mathbb{Z}^d$ can be expressed as a subgroup of a characteristic random subgroup of an abelian group, possessing properties of weak mixing and faithfulness. Consequentially, a random topological group, resulting from this characteristic subgroup, inherits the same characteristics of weak mixing and faithfulness.

We analyze the internal dynamics of quasi neural networks, a broad class of
networks, including those with ReLU and 1-Lipschitz activations. Our analysis
focuses on the neural tangent kernel (NTK), a linear approximation of the
quasi neural network, and reveals two critical features. Firstly, we observe that
the NTK converges to a Gramian of a certain Hilbert space as iterations progress,
and, secondly, we establish that the eigenvalues decay at a geometric rate.
Building on these findings, we demonstrate that quasi neural networks, when viewed
through the NTK lens, exhibit a regularized behavior, and, depending on the decay
rate of the eigenvalue, either converge to a smooth regression function or
experience diminishing amplitude while increasing frequency. Our analysis
encompasses an in-depth case study of 1-Lipschitz networks, a broad class that
enables precise estimation of the decay rate of the eigenvalue, and, as a
consequence, yields a novel algorithm for optimizing these networks that
significantly improves upon prior methods.

Quantum information processing's foundation is built on understanding entropy's constraints, particularly after tensoring operations. For partitioned systems, determining whether applied entropies exceed what's allowed can lead to valuable insights, even if the entropies themselves don't necessarily describe the entire system. For bulk regions of systems undergoing tensoring operations, a higher boundary entropy on average is allowed than for individual systems. However, whether this allowance necessarily translates to higher boundary entropy generally remains unclear. In this work, we explore the allowance for bulk entropies in terms of mutual information constraints and show that allowing higher boundary entropies generally requires non-monogamy of information within the bulk. A higher boundary entropy is then allowed on average. Demonstrating non-monogamy of information in bulk regions typically involves information being shared among more than two parties, not just individual parties. In holographic theories, this information takes the form of geometric entanglements. In this work, we display a more subtle non-monogamy of information in bulk regions through diverging pages of entanglement spectra. Each page of an entangled spectrum represents information shared between a particular pair of boundary segments. A higher boundary entropy is allowed on average when the information shared between certain pairs of boundaries is maximally entangled with each other, whereas diverging pages indicate non-monogamy of information shared within the bulk between those same boundary segments.

This investigation focuses on deriving a branching rule for a specific, solvable lattice model called the spin-one restricted face model, built on a square grid in D dimensions. To achieve this, we first convert the model into a tiling on a D-dimensional hypercube called a Pompelon, comprising hexagonal and triangular sections. By applying a set of moves that maintain energy.

We establish a correspondence between the symmetries of the Pompelon and the Weyl group of the Lie algebra D. We then define a set of characters associated with the branching rule, which represent local state probabilities within the spin-one restricted face model. These character probabilities can be expressed in terms of the branching rule for the general spin-restricted face model in D dimensions.

We derive local state probability expressions for the spin-one restricted face model in D dimensions, based on a conjectured general spin-restricted face model branching rule in D dimensions. These probability expressions match known results for D = 2 and D = 3.

We propose an iterative method for calculating the branching rule of the spin-one restricted face model in D dimensions, by combining results from lower-dimensional cases. This iteration could potentially be used to calculate the branching rule for less solvable models.

This research investigates how the integration of various stabilization methods affects recovery algorithms. Specifically, we analyzed the impact of combining specialized techniques, such as the iterative shrinkage thresholding method and the conditional mean feedback algorithm, under stabilized conditions. Our findings demonstrate that the simultaneous application of multiple stabilization methods can significantly influence the performance of recovery algorithms. In contrast to individual stabilizations, which typically ensure unique and optimal solutions, we identified instances where combining stabilizations led to non-unique solutions. Consequently, we advocate for a data-dependent selection of stabilizations to enhance algorithm effectiveness.

Our previous studies revealed that nonlinear coaddition methods like median and clipped-mean preserve signal but not spatial resolution, by often suppressing more than half of the information in each frame. This led us to explore alternative nonlinear techniques, such as using parametric distributions, specifically the normal and log-normal, to better accommodate data contrasts. Based on these findings, we suggest examining the properties of specific nonlinear combinations of coaddition and clipping algorithms. Ultimately, our research aims to provide insight into the extent to which achieving both strong signal preservation and consistent point spread function (PSF) profiles is feasible.

We introduce the chordal SLE driven by a Borel measure on the Riemann sphere minus three points, and show it satisfies a certain evolution equation. Its imaginary component resembles the chordal Loewner evolution with a driving measure that can be derived from a Borel measure on the Riemann sphere minus three points. By examining its properties, we demonstrate that chordal SLE represents the uniformization theorem for certain domains on the Riemann sphere. On top of that, we establish a duality theorem between SLE(2) and chordal SLE, and use this to determine the asymptotic behavior of a family of functions related to SLE(2) and current calculations in the context of conformal field theories. Furthermore, we define the radial SLE driven by a Borel measure on the unit circle and in the upper half-plane, and establish its essential properties. We also introduce the unique evolving domain associated with any given driving measure and prove it meets specific conditions. By taking a special measure, we obtain the classical Loewner evolution, thereby providing an alternative explanation for its properties. Ultimately, our findings allow us to address the question of whether SLE(2) is conformally invariant, considering recent results involving the relationship between SLE and conformal field theories.

We establish a nonlocal estimate for the solution and its derivatives of the 2D Navier-Stokes equations, based on the maximum norm of the initial conditions, in a domain with irregular boundaries. Specifically, it's shown that the maximum norm of the solution's derivatives at time T is bounded by a constant times the maximum norm of the initial conditions, raised to the power of 1/α, in a domain extending α hours into the past. To derive this result, we follow the standard procedure of introducing an averaged element along the timeline. However, the resulting integral is nonlocal due to the integration time, requiring an alternative approach to bound it. We apply the integration by parts technique to limit the temporal integration area to the \alphaT interval, then utilize the Cauchy inequality and the Helmholtz decomposition to derive the desired estimate.

This paper proposes an improved complex-valued quantum computation verification protocol, CVQC. It leverages the advantages of both phase estimation and the standard quantum simulation, yet yields significantly faster verification at a fraction of the cost compared to existing protocols. Interestingly, the same technique can also be applied to zero-knowledge proof systems; our CVQC protocol actually simplifies the existing zk-SNARKs validation process while aligning with quantum computing. Our CVQC protocol comes with theoretical guarantees of both constant factor and asymptotic efficiency improvements over the current best protocols. Furthermore, our experiments demonstrate that, at this moment, the CVQC protocol is still within practical limits of constant factor inefficiency but is poised to become more efficient as future developments in quantum computing unfold.

The synthetic data generated by deep generative models can be used to create virtual datasets, while also improving image analysis tools. For our project, we combined a cell shape synthesis using a Variational Autoencoder (VAE) and a cell tracking algorithm based on a Dynamic Time Warping (DTW) metric. The goal was to see if synthesizing cell shapes and tracking them could lead to better results, especially in difficult cases. To do this, we compared the performance of our combined system with a regular DTW tracking method, and found that it produced more accurate tracking in hard situations without affecting performance in easier cases. The code and synthesized data used in this research have been made available on GitHub at https://github.com/jmcmcmcmc/VAE_DTW_tracking.

Reinforcement Learning research has focused primarily on the relationships between environment dynamics and suboptimal policy mercury, but little has been focused on the effects of other environmental characteristics.  A new analysis reveals that feature persistence - the extent to which environment features remain unchanged - significantly influences geometric task performance.  Feature persistence is found to be closely correlated with the eigenvalues of the environment's transition matrix, and a binary classification criterion for persistent features is established.  It is proven that persistent features hinder convergence of geometric reinforcement learning algorithms and demonstrate the need for faster exploration rates in order to achieve convergence in high-persistence environments.  Existing literature may have underestimated the impact of feature persistence, as it is often approximately zero in commonly studied grid-worlds and cliffwalking scenarios while reaching up to 0.99 in simple geometric tasks like navigating a circle or a torus.  A potential framework for distinguishing between tasks that require focus on geometric properties versus those suitable for reinforcement learning mercury is presented.

The Eckart-Cohen-Mosselachini (ECMC) algorithm is renowned for unlocking collective behavior in complex models, yet its application to three-dimensional dipolar particles is hindered by a fundamental issue: dynamical arrest. A revised Newtonian ECMC (NECMC) method successfully bypasses this obstacle in three-dimensional dipolar systems by leveraging the zero-flux theorem. In simulations, NECMC produced fast convergence to equilibrium in various dipolar particle configurations, outperforming previous methods. The underlying reasoning involves eliminating non-conservative innovations in updates, thus preserving the zero-flux property and enabling long-term simulation viability. The NECMC variant has the potential to revolutionize conservative stochastic modeling by addressing conservative arithmetic errors.

This paper reports on data augmentation methods used during training for a sound event detection system, specifically designed to identify bird species from audio recordings. A range of techniques was employed to expand the dataset, including signal-level modifications and feature vector transformation. Results reveal that while some methods slightly hinder performance, others significantly boost the accuracy of the classification model. A notable discovery was the substantial improvement yielded by generating supplementary training data through label-guided approaches. Notably, the best performing method achieved an increase of 0.04 in F-score, with the benefit being particularly pronounced for less common bird species. Consequently, data augmentation is recommended as an effective strategy for enhancing sound event detection systems.

The principle of superposition in wireless communications allows multiple signals to coexist at the receiver. This property underpins various technologies, such as superposition diversity, federated learning, and non-orthogonal multiple access (NOMA). A new technique, called superposition coding with partial channel state information, supports multiple users in wireless networks. This method is being evaluated for use in 5G New Radio (5G NR) and beyond. There has been limited exploration of its security vulnerabilities. We have developed a comprehensive analysis of an existing system that uses superposition coding with partial CSI and max ratio combining (MRC) and its decentralized version with artificial noise (AN) and mode selection (MS). Our main contributions are: Firstly, we have established a comprehensive decoding strategy for an untrusted receiver in the classic superposition coding system with MRC. To our knowledge, this is the first such comprehensive decoding strategy presented in the literature. Secondly, we have introduced a novel and powerful decoding strategy for the existing and decentralized superposition coding systems with AN and MS. Our third contribution has been the correlation based decoding strategy for the nominal and decentralized superposition coding systems with MRC. We have further refined our decoding strategies for the nominal and decentralized superposition coding systems with MRC, and demonstrated that our newly proposed strategies outperform previously reported alternatives.

This paper investigates a spectrogram analysis problem, presenting a theoretical foundation for a family of signal detection and estimation techniques based on level sets. These techniques, including the Spectrogram Level Sets (SLs) and its enhanced version with prior information (SLI), are rooted in the Spectrogram Level Sets algorithm. We demonstrate that SLs and SLI represent specific instances of the General Level Set Algorithm (GLSA), while also showing that Spectrogram CUSUM and its enhanced version with prior information (CUSUMI) can be viewed as iterative applications of GLSA. Our analysis reveals that both Spectrogram CUSUM and SLs achieve the optimal asymptotic performance, although Spectrogram CUSUM incurs the highest computational cost. Conversely, Spectrogram CUSUM may experience suboptimal performance due to its iteration-based approach. In contrast, SLI and the enhanced General Level Set Algorithm (GLS) exhibit computational efficiency by bypassing the iteration requirement. Our results also illustrate the statistical performance limitations of SL and its potential improvement with prior information, supporting our proposal for the Spectrogram Level Sets with Prior (SLIP) as the most efficient estimator among the considered techniques.

We examine a generalized Allen-Cahn system in a specified domain and analyze its periodic and synchronized states. These states are characterized by distinct groups of oscillations, known as synchronized clusters, which exist within the system. Through a combination of geometric and analytical methods, we identify the number of these clusters and show how their boundaries separate distinct regions within the system's parameter space. Furthermore, we establish the existence of periodic solutions and their stability under specified conditions and demonstrate that, as one of the system's dimensions becomes large, a particular type of synchronized cluster dominates, resulting in a sharp transition boundary within the system's parameter space.

We introduce a novel Python module named PhysModules, which enables the simulation of physical systems characterized by particle motion. This module segregates logical aspects from implementation details, enabling users to model complex physical phenomena through high-level descriptions. It offers a range of innovative features, including visual representation, automated generation of numerical methods, and seamless integration with existing simulation frameworks. The efficacy of this module is demonstrated through its application in modeling and simulating droplet motion within various systems.

The traditional second law of thermodynamics is often assessed through the information engine known as the Maxwell demon, which relies on discrete quantum measurements. However, real-world measurements are continuous and sequential. Therefore, it is essential to reevaluate the second law by incorporating continuous quantum measurements. This study investigates the information engine model with continuous quantum measurement and non-invasive measurement approaches. It is revealed that continuous quantum measurements do not provide a benefit in enhancing the engine's efficiency, and the second law is not violated. Moreover, the information engine's performance is not substantially enhanced when compared to a scenario without quantum effects. This finding suggests that the traditional understanding of the Maxwell demon is relevant in contemporary quantum technology applications.

In a study on the mechanics of dense disk packs, researchers used 3D printing and electronic loading to examine jamming phenomena in a confined environment.  The disks were made of different materials, ranging from extremely light to heavy, weighing less than 1 gram per square millimeter.  With advanced electronic loading, they applied forces to the disks in various directions while taking precise measurements of the disk pack's deformation under load.  The results showed that lighter disks jam more easily and at a lower applied force than heavier disks.  This behavior contradicts earlier theories on jamming and suggests a new direction for research in the mechanics of complex materials.

Research indicates that various forms of El Niño and La Niña have distinct impacts on global precipitation patterns. To differentiate between these flavors, researchers can rely on sensitive precipitation sensors or estimate them by analyzing satellite data on total precipitation. By examining flavor-specific precipitation patterns, researchers have identified regions where their differences have significant implications for predicting extreme weather events. To develop an accurate approach, researchers train a machine learning model using climate data from 1981 to 2000, focusing on distinct total precipitation patterns and their links to temperature anomalies. When evaluated against historical climate data from 2001 to 2015, this novel approach yielded promising results. To ensure the model's reliability, researchers repeated the analysis and found the results to be consistent across different datasets and techniques. This distinct flavor classification method may hold potential for enhancing climate pattern identification and predicting extreme weather events.

The earliest black hole seeds in heavy seed theories are thought to have formed large masses, typically above $10^9$ solar masses, whereas light seeding scenarios assume smaller masses, typically around $10^6$ solar masses. To understand the mass spectrum of heavy seeds, we studied the merger history of black holes within dark matter minihalos using the consistent lattice field theory and simple analytic models. Our findings show that there is a significant range of possible masses, ranging from approximately $10^6$ to $10^{10}$ solar masses, with the average mass and distribution depending on various parameters such as the number of minihalo mergers and accretion efficiency. This work sheds light on the mass spectrum of heavy seeds and the potential mass range for supermassive black holes, existing black holes, and dark matter particles.

Recent research has focused heavily on the properties of flat band-driven correlations in complex systems, particularly those with multiple orbital characteristics. A recent study introduced a new model, featuring a lattice structure consisting of interlinked triangular rings on a honeycomb substrate, to examine correlation effects in flat bands. By combining wave-like patterns and flat bands into a single framework, the study identified key features, such as spin correlation patterns and band structures. Additionally, the study derived an effective Hamiltonian and explored the correlation effects within the framework of an effective lattice. As a result, the study revealed the emergence of correlation-driven phenomena, encompassing areas such as flat band-induced pairing and unusual correlation-driven patterns of spin and charge.

Using a combination of protein sequences and expression data, we developed a method to quantify how individual SNPs contribute to cell type-specific expression levels. Applying this approach to 30 human cell types and 49 publicly available datasets, we found that the impact of protein sequence on phenotype-associated SNPs differed significantly across different traits, with the median variation ranging from 10% to 60%. Furthermore, we demonstrated that considering the protein sequence of transcription factors enhances our ability to forecast the effects of genotype on gene expression, resulting in a 15% average improvement across all cell types. Finally, we provided a simplified representation of the complex interactions involved in regulating gene expression by highlighting the key positions in the transcription factor protein that significantly contribute to predicting expression level changes caused by SNPs.

In this research, we establish that a $2$-design with a prime power number of points and a nontrivial automorphism group must have a cycle of singlets under its group action. We utilize this finding to address the squaring conjecture for $2$-designs, confirming its truth for prime power point counts but refracting it into separate cases for pairs of cycles that are either similar or dissimilar.

Within the Hohenberg-Kohn theory, electronic entropy is defined as the maximum thermodynamic quantity subject to Hohenberg-Kohn conditions. It measures the imperfection of the invariance transformation generated by the Coulomb correlation in a many-electron system. It has been proven that entropy bears a systematic relationship with Coulomb correlation effects, which diminishes as particles are confined in smaller spatial areas. This relationship holds for both Coulomb correlation effects within HFK and non-local correlation effects within NKFK. Furthermore, it has been demonstrated that the entropy change upon confining a system is positive, whereas the energy change may be either positive or negative, depending on the characteristics of the confining potential. This has been verified for (a) a hydrogenic atomic system bounded by a Coulomb potential and (b) a sodium atomic system bounded by a Coulomb potential, within a cylindrical potential well.

The binary star system HD 150383 was observed at four epochs between 2009 and 2015 using the SBSOIC camera and the 1.0 meter telescope at the Xinglong Station of the National Astronomical Observatory. Its data was analyzed to determine the velocity of each star in the binary pair, allowing for a more accurate measurement of their velocity dispersion. This new approach for analyzing wide binary star systems could provide a valuable tool for testing theories of gravitational physics by offering a more precise test of gravitational non-linearity.

We introduce a method for translating the meaning of formulas in multiplicative linear logic into group theory, allowing for an interpretation of the logic through the behavior of group elements. We observe that ideal representations comply with the principles of cut-elimination and connectivism, revealing a deeper structural aspect. Furthermore, we establish a duality between formula meanings and proof constructs, revealing that the latter can be explicitly modeled as group operations. This framework provides a precise semantic foundation for the logic, and our analysis provides new insights into the cut-elimination theorem.

Our study explores the complex dynamics of time series coupling, focusing on predicting the synchronization status of pairs of time series. We employ a multilayer perceptron trained on time series similarity features and demonstrate that it excels at predicting synchronization, yielding a 73% true positive rate, a 43% true negative rate, and significant 5% and 8% prediction errors for in-synchronized and out-of-sync time series, respectively. Building on previous work, our approach involves analyzing the time series relationships for FX pairs using a new time series similarity feature and predicting the synchronization status. We conduct two experiments, determining the features' discriminative power and the robustness of our model, and reveal that deep learning outperforms a linear support vector machine, offering enhanced prediction accuracy and robustness.

To effectively regulate chemical reactions, controlling vibrational states is crucial. This can be achieved by leveraging quantum effects that strengthen the reaction driving force. Given the challenges associated with directly manipulating atomic positions, it's essential to explore alternative pathways, such as influencing vibrational modes that are coupled to quantum states. An exciting prospect arises from the application of Floquet engineering, which enables the creation of permanent vibrations by limiting a system to specific radiofrequency driving frequencies. This study investigates the creation of long-lasting vibrational modes in a bipyridine diiron complex, an important molecular oracle for hydrogen evolution and oxygen activation. By applying Floquet driving forces, it's possible to create periodic vibrations that enhance electrical activation of the diiron center, potentially facilitating oxygen activation. This study examines how Floquet driving forces influence the electronic structure and, via density functional analysis, predicts that periodic vibrations can lower the oxygen binding energy and increase the oxygen-to-iron distance. Ultimately, this research offers a new direction for quantum control over chemical reactions, enabling the development of more efficient electrocatalysts.

Recent click-through rate (CTR) prediction models in online advertising often overlook visual factors, yet they hold significant potential for growth. To address this gap, our research introduces a new type of feature: Visual ID, which serves as a universal and standardized identifier for ad visuals. By combining Visual ID with historical click data, our analysis reveals improved accuracy in click-through rate prediction, particularly in new and sparse scenarios. To create this Visual ID, our team developed a unique Ad Visual Embedding (AVE) that represents the visual content of ads using a unified, high-dimensional space, effectively capturing the visual appearance and semantics of ads, thus serving as a Visual ID. Experimental results validate the effectiveness of the proposed model.

The introduction of fairness constraints in business process management, particularly with regard to fairness in resource usage, has been under-explored. Current approaches focus solely on achieving a resource-intensive fair schedule but overlook the importance of meeting resource quantity requirements. To bridge this gap, a new fairness assessment criterion, denoted as $\mathring{f}$, is introduced, enabling the evaluation of business process models according to both resource usage equity and quantity compliance. Moreover, the problem of generating a fair business process instance, given a process model and a resource pool, is formally defined and initially tackled under the assumption of infinite process execution. For this specific case, an algorithm based on the linear programming method is developed to derive the minimum number of process cycles required, subsequently demonstrating the algorithm's infeasibility in certain situations. The concepts and techniques introduced provide a foundational framework for the theoretical analysis of fairness in business process instances.

The past year has seen numerous wildfires raging in Australia that have had a significant impact on air quality, with hazardous particulate matter affecting communities and airports. To accurately predict the transport of airborne pollutants from these fires, we need to model their propagation. Given the complex interactions involved, reliable statistical methods are well-suited to filling the knowledge gap. Building on existing research, we have adapted the Advection-Diffusion-Oxygen-Dependence equations to create an AOD model. This model, which takes into account the variables of particulate matter ($p$), velocity ($v$), and oxygen ($O$), is being used to generate synthetic data. By incorporating data from both the Adelaide and Canberra airports, we have created probabilistic models for each location using the AOD equations and Bayesian neural networks. These models have been validated through cross-validation and comparison with actual air quality data, with promising results that demonstrate the ability to make accurate predictions over short distances.

Privacy preservation in location-based services is crucial for maintaining user anonymity. Currently used methods rely on synthetic data creation by transforming true positive records into negative ones, but fail to account for data conditioned on past records. Our proposed framework addresses this shortfall by introducing a privacy framework that utilizes relevance maps to maintain privacy for conditioned data. It relies on generating private relevance maps for data points by grouping them into clusters based on their similarities and assigning a synthetic relevance map to each cluster. Each data point is then connected to the relevance map of its corresponding cluster, providing consistent relevance maps for data of the same type. This framework maintains privacy for data conditioned on past records and ensures privacy for data of the same type. It also maintains privacy for data of the same location and time. Moreover, it maintains privacy for data of the same user. Our proposed framework also maintains k-nearest neighbors for data of the same location and time. It also maintains $l$-diversity for data of the same location. This framework achieves privacy for data of the same location by adjusting the relevance maps of some data points and maintaining diversity for data of the the same location. Deciphering the dynamic brain connections that underlie cognitive processes and behavioral disorders is a key goal of functional magnetic resonance imaging. However, individual variations in brain functions are complex and multi-scale. Despite decades of research, it remains unclear which brain connections are critical for reliable observations. Using a simulation network that mimics real brain interactions, our study examines how inter-site effects influence the reliability of detecting individual and group differences. Our results indicate that site-specific effects are essential for reliable observations and differ significantly across brain connections. Consequently, individual differences are predominantly identified at shorter temporal scales, whereas group differences are prominent at longer scales. Notably, considering inter-site effects enhances the accuracy of detecting both individual and group differences. Ultimately, this knowledge encourages the use of dynamic causal models for further exploring brain mechanisms underpinning cognitive processes and disorders.

We have established a heat-based formulation of concentration of measure inequalities.
Our generalized entropy inequality builds upon prior work by the same authors, and we
have derived a functional form of entropy inequalities for specific functions.
This leads to the creation of concentration of measure inequalities, and we
have explored applications within non-smooth potential theory.

Recent advancements in self-supervised pre-training for code-mixed language models have led to remarkable accuracy in zero-shot and multi-lingual text classification tasks. Nonetheless, existing approaches predominantly focus on modeling multi-lingual and cross-lingual characteristics, while neglecting the significance of positional encoding for code-mixed text. Our innovative model, MixEnc, addresses this gap by integrating a novel positional encoding technique specifically designed for code-mixed sequences. This new encoding technique distills the inherent properties of code-mixed language into numerical representations. Our thorough experiments on three extensively used datasets - IndoNLP, IUL and TATO - showcase the superior performance of MixEnc in comparison to state-of-the-art models, highlighting its overall effectiveness and robustness. Moreover, ablation studies and detailed analyses reveal that using multi-lingual and positional encoding leads to better performance than solely utilizing multi-lingual characteristics. Consequently, MixEnc outperforms existing models across various dataset and task configurations.

The isotope effect coefficient in H$_{3}$S and its analogs is composed of two components, which are distinct from the isotope effect coefficient in hydrogen-rich materials. By studying the isotope effect coefficient in H$_{3}$S and its relationship with pressure, we identified a strong dependence on electron-phonon interaction under high pressure. Furthermore, our calculations predict that the negative value of the isotope effect coefficient in H$_{3}$S will shift to a positive value at pressures exceeding 25 GPa, which aligns with the findings of experimental studies under high pressure conditions. By analyzing the isotope effect coefficient in H$_{3}$S and its analogs, we obtained key insights into the structural and phase transition mechanisms in these materials.

In evolutionary biology, measuring genes' influence on the phenome to understand genetic effects has been challenging.  Despite numerous studies using quantitative genetics, estimating the average effect of a single gene substitution on a trait has remained an unsolved problem.  We addressed this issue by developing new methods and applying them to yeast and Drosdelisela melanogaster data sets.  Our analysis revealed that the average effect of a single gene substitution within a species is essentially zero.  This finding holds true regardless of whether the genes are coding or non-coding, and is consistent across multiple functional categories.  We propose that the average effect of a single gene substitution should serve as a standard unit to measure a gene's influence on a particular trait.  We further provide evidence that the average effect of a single gene substitution is linked to the direction of the gene's impact on the trait.  In contrast, the magnitude of the gene effect is better explained by random genetic variations than by known genetic factors.  Our study identifies key distinctions between mean effects and variances in evolutionary biology, thereby offering new insights into the biology of genetic effects.

This study proposes a nonlinear controller based on nonlinear hysteretic feedback
(NHF) control to manage a bipedal robot's degeneration during gait cycles. NHF control
combines feedback and feedforward signals to ensure the bipedal robot remains in sync
with an intended trajectory. To tackle the identically distributed degeneration that
arises when only a feedback signal is utilized, our research develops a predictive model
based on the Lotka-Volterra equation to estimate the impact of temporal discrepancy on
the bipedal robot's degeneration. Simulation results reveal that our proposed nonlinear
hysteretic feedback control can lower the bipedal robot's degeneration to the point where
it no longer increases over time. Additionally, we found that there is an optimal threshold for
temporal discrepancy to optimize gait performance while minimizing degeneration.

We introduce a groundbreaking method to train camera descriptors using 3D point clouds generated from synthetic data, and demonstrate its exceptional performance using real-world images and point clouds. This approach leverages learned descriptors to match feature points between images and 3D point clouds, and has been designed to thrive in difficult lighting conditions. To optimize our method's efficiency, we developed an innovative point cloud sampling strategy that selectively uses more points from areas that have been previously detected as relevant for pose estimation. This technique significantly improves our model's performance by minimizing unnecessary computations. Empirical tests conducted on the KITTI dataset confirm that our method outperforms or matches the best existing results for monocular and stereo camera pose estimation, while being up to 2.5 times faster than the current top-performing deep learning-based methods. We have released our code and demo on the following website: <https://github.com/alegrosotto/pointcloud_desc>.

In the personalization domain of federated learning, a semi-supervised model is simultaneously created, allowing for adjustments to be made based on personal data.  However, with personal datasets being relatively small, personal semi-supervised models often suffer from a lack of sufficient unlabeled data and limited labeled data compared to a global model, leading to reduced performance.  This paper proposes a novel technique to enhance the personal semi-supervised learning process by increasing the availability of unlabeled data for personal models.  A personal data augmentation model is first created using a few labeled data, then utilized to create additional personal examples.  A new personal semi-supervised learning framework is then developed to combine these personal examples and labeled data, resulting in improved performance.  This approach is compared to existing personal learning methods through various numerical experiments under both independent and dependent data conditions.  Finally, the effects of varying label scarcity on personal semi-supervised learning models are numerically evaluated.

The disintegration of a neutron star following a binary merger leads to a significant reduction in magnetic field strength within the resulting accretion disk. Recent studies indicate that magnetic field decay occurs primarily during the initial stages of the merger, with older neutron stars exhibiting more resilient magnetic fields. Prior theories suggested that magnetic field elimination required an elaborate process involving magnetic field instabilities and reconnection. Unlike previous predictions, new observations suggest that early post-merger magnetic field dynamics might be less complex than expected, with systems like GW170817 exhibiting reduced magnetic fields through less elaborate mechanisms. Consequently, magnetic field fluctuations become more pronounced as they are sustained throughout the accretion disk phase, with little to no initial resistance. With a greater understanding of magnetic field behavior, researchers can create more accurate simulations of post-merger systems, including their observational impacts on short gamma-ray bursts and gravitational waves.

For a compact Riemann surface, its virtual class can be defined through a specific mathematical structure, involving a point-pairing operation between the surface and itself. This can be done in two different ways, leading to the first and second Mumford-Morita-Miller classes. These pairings are closely related to the algebraic properties of the surface's Chow ring and its dual. We have found a way to simplify the definition of the first class, reducing it to a more basic mathematical concept. Additionally, we have discovered a relationship between the second class and the point-pairing operation, showing that it can be expressed as the product of two other mathematical classes, rather than a more complex intersection. This finding provides new insights into the geometric properties of compact Riemann surfaces.

This study establishes conditions for a Markov process to have an exclusive quasi-stationary distribution that converges exponentially, in combination with irreducibility and a dominant stationary distribution. The underlying theory involves two primary conditions on the Markov process: (i) it must have a unique quasi-stationary distribution that converges exponentially, in combination with a specific growth rate, and (ii) it must avoid certain pathological states that can disrupt its asymptotic behavior. As an enabler of this theory, we first prove that any ergodic Markov process with certain symmetry properties has an exclusive quasi-stationary distribution that converges exponentially, under conditions of weak irreducibility and certain boundedness constraints on its transition rates. As specific applications of these results, we prove the exponential convergence of a Markov process with an exclusive quasi-stationary distribution in two distinct scenarios: (a) when it has a unique ergodic distribution and certain symmetry properties, and (b) when it has a unique ergodic distribution and certain boundedness properties, and we also prove the exponential convergence of a large class of reversible jump processes, including discrete and continuous processes, and diffusion processes with multiple equilibrium states. Furthermore, we establish that any ergodic Markov process with an exclusive quasi-stationary distribution that converges exponentially must have certain growth rate properties and, under certain regularity conditions, must also have an exponential rate of convergence in its ergodic distribution. Finally, we provide counterexamples to demonstrate the complexity of

Optical forces exerting a gentle pressure on graphene can fine-tune the equilibrium positions of particles suspended above it. The graphene's chemical potential can be adjusted to control these movements. In this research, we have conducted a thorough analysis of the radio-frequency guided waves within double-layered herringbone nanostructures composed of silicon nitride and graphene. Our findings show that changing the chemical potential of graphene causes non-reciprocal propagation of these waves. The graphene's chemical potential was studied in detail, and we found that altering it not only leads to different equilibrium positions but also causes permanent changes in the properties of the system. Our results also indicate that non-reciprocal transmission can be achieved at specific frequencies, and this can be enhanced by adjusting the gap height between the layers.

To determine the optimal Emergency Department (ED) length of stay, we estimated the association between treatment time and post-discharge healthcare utilization. By analyzing a large patient dataset from a US health network, we found that a 30-minute increase in treatment time was associated with a 0.5 to 1.5 percentage point increase in ED revisit rates and a 0.5 to 1.5 percentage point increase in readmission rates within 30 days. Due to potential biases, we also controlled for the patient's propensity to visit the ED. By developing and applying a propensity score-based confidence interval method, we adjusted for common confounders and isolated the causal impact of treatment time. Our findings suggest that increasing treatment time leads to higher rates of healthcare utilization, supporting the claim that the optimal ED length of stay is shorter than the current standard.

We examine how a collaborative multi-agent system makes decisions in response to varying difficulties of tasks. These tasks are represented by specific values that influence the system's objectives, and each agent has a distinct preference for tackling tasks with specific value ranges. We analyze how a group of self-interested agents without access to each other's preferences makes decisions in a sequential setting, where each agent takes a task based on its own preferences and the current state of the system. We investigate how the distribution of task difficulties affects the outcome in both a system where tasks are infinite and a setting with a finite number of tasks. We relate the resulting joint action of the agents to a corresponding equilibrium in a corresponding game that is played simultaneously. Our analysis offers insights into how the distribution of task difficulties affects the performance of collaborative multi-agent systems and provides a basis for making decisions in such systems.

Research focuses on understanding how quark properties influence the creation of particles in collisions. Studies rely on a measure called "correlation functions," which are derived from the angle at which particles are detected. In new investigations, analysts considered how events without specific charges influence the measurement of these correlations. They discovered that events without charges not only provide expected insights but also reveal details about the way particles are linked. The findings suggest an increased need for events without charges in the analysis of particle collisions and offer a new method for extracting information from such events. Analysts further explored whether it's possible to eliminate the influence of events without charges by adjusting how these events are weighted. The conclusions suggest this approach has the potential to refine measurements but would likely be difficult to put into practice.

This study introduces a multifaceted approach to predicting crowdfunding outcomes
based on project characteristics and creator backgrounds, crowdfunders. Unlike other
models that concentrate on project-related variables, we synthesize crowd behavior
observed during project launches, synthesizing information gathered from project
description, financial reports, creator profiles, and historical data. This is done
by incorporating a crowd dynamics feature in our model. Using data from Kickstarter
and a strategy for selecting relevant variables, we investigated how well different
features can forecast project success and funding amounts. Notably, the crowd
dynamics feature exhibited comparable predictive power to other variables. Consequently,
our research suggests that crowd behavior is a valuable source of information for
predicting project outcomes. Furthermore, we propose a crowd-driven strategy for
targeted advertising, suggesting that crowdfunders could be encouraged to support
projects with characteristics similar to those that received high funding in relation to
the crowdfunder's own preferences.

Innovations in IoT have expanded across industries, yet their security is shrouded in uncertainty. To mitigate this, organizations are adopting Intrusion Detection Systems, with some partnering to share knowledge. Although beneficial, this sharing comes with privacy risks, prompting a need for secure and private knowledge sharing among organizations. To address this, a federated learning framework has been proposed, allowing multiple organizations to collaboratively train a common model while maintaining local data privacy through periodic aggregation. This approach, however, was found to unfavorably affect model performance when fed pseudo-anonymized data alone, especially in intrusion detection tasks. To rectify this, a federated learning system was designed to integrate with existing IDS systems, allowing multiple organizations to train a common model on their respective datasets and achieve satisfactory performance. A key component of this architecture is a federated learning engine, responsible for organizing the training process, and a customized Python library, facilitating communication among organizations via REST APIs. To address dataset disparities, a dataset normalizer was developed to process and prepare datasets for training, while a federated learning wrapper was used to integrate FL into existing IDS systems. To ensure seamless integration, a decision was made to use existing IDS models, updating them only when participating in the FL process. This decision is based on the trade-off between performance and computational overhead. To combat non-uniform updates during training, a decision was made to use online federated learning updates, allowing organizations to maintain their existing infrastructure. Recent advancements in optimal path planning have been focused on selecting the most efficient task sequence. This work builds upon the E* algorithm, a popular path planning algorithm, and adapts it for autonomous robotic applications by integrating it into a single algorithm, the SE* algorithm. This adaptation enables the detection of task exceptions or disruptions, causing a re-evaluation of the route and task sequence for optimal execution. By maintaining a memory of previous states, the SE* algorithm can quickly recover from disruptions, leading to a 45% faster recovery time compared to alternative methods. Furthermore, task exceptions result in a 14% faster overall execution time than planned tasks.

The primary factor influencing the mobility of metal-oxide-semiconductor devices is the characteristics of the gate material. In this study, various gate materials were examined to assess their suitability for enhancing the mobility of MOS devices. A range of gate materials, including HfO$_2$/TiN, ZrO$_2$/TGdW, and LaAlO$_3$/TOX, were looked into and compared with the standard gate material, HfO$_2$/TiN. Furthermore, the study explored the potential of using ultra-thin gate materials, specifically 1 nm and 2 nm HfO$_2$, and evaluated the performance with different choice of gate metal, comparing TiN and GdTa. A thorough investigation into the source of threshold voltage shift was conducted on 5 nm MOS transistors featuring HfO$_2$/TiN technology, and the findings showed that the voltage shift can be effectively minimized through the optimization of the gate process.

We studied how additive noise influences the stability of complex patterns in a network of oscillators where individual nodes receive information about their neighbors through a time-delayed information system. Our analysis revealed that although long periods of synchronization may occur, they are unstable and susceptible to disruptions. We observed that when system parameters are precise, they can facilitate stable synchronization, but even slight variations can lead to the demise of the pattern. Our findings were confirmed through numerical simulations, which showed that a high level of noise does not necessarily cause the collapse of the pattern, but rather it takes time. Our results have significant implications for understanding synchronization in biological and climate systems.

Between 2018 and 2020, researchers conducted an investigation into how Western online search engines respond to queries that may suggest YouTube results. The researchers looked for any evidence of YouTube's presence in the output, particularly when querying terms that are more commonly associated with the video platform. The data from this study revealed an interesting trend: while YouTube's presence could sometimes be inferred from other sources, such as metadata or links, the actual number of queries that yielded YouTube results decreased over the studied time period across multiple search engines. Given that YouTube is now widely recognized as the largest video library in the world, the researchers note that excluding Video Search Engine Results Pages (VESRs) from overall traffic may lead to an inaccurate understanding of the true usage of these search engines. The data from this study could offer insights into how to correctly categorize traffic associated with the largest video library in the world.

When a topological quantum field theory is equipped with general monodromy defects, the $\beta$-function exhibits a unique behavior compared to its bare counterpart. We've derived a comprehensive mathematical framework in this study to analyze the effects of these defects on the $\beta$-function for quantizations associated with symmetric pairs of Lie algebras. We've also demonstrated specific instances of how the $\beta$-function is modified by 4D supersymmetric theories subjected to various defects.

In our study, we consider a cubic Galois field extension, and an elliptic curve defined over this field. We establish certain conditions under which the elliptic curve's properties in the extended field can be determined based on its $K$-rational point of order 13. This enables us to count the number of $K$-rational points of order 13. Subsequently, we apply these findings to understand how many $K$-rational points of order 13 an elliptic curve may have given a specific condition, and derive a statement about prime-order points on elliptic curves over certain fields.

The temporal characteristics of network delays are disregarded in existing analysis techniques for delay-based network protocols. This research introduces an approach to analyze the statistics of delay-based protocol instances by considering the local delay ratio, θ, that compares to the network delay σ. Based on θ and σ, four operation modes - pure stochastic, random sampling, synchronous, and timing-driven - are identified. An empirical model is developed to represent the delay distribution in each mode and is supported by both theoretical and experimental evaluations. The model exhibits excellent matching with measured data across various distribution types, but our findings also indicate that many protocols operate in a pure stochastic mode despite being non-exponential.

Semi-supervised node classification in graph neural networks can be vulnerable to data distribution shifts and rare category data due to over-reliance on pseudo-labeled data. Traditional pseudo-labeling methods, which assign labels to unsupervised nodes based on their predicted confidence levels, can exacerbate a model's existing biases, leading to pseudo-labeled nodes primarily consisting of easily identifiable nodes that also happen to be the most predictive nodes for the target labels. As a result, the model is effectively reinforced with additional, biased data. This paper addresses this limitation by introducing a novel pseudo-labeling technique. Unlike prior methods, which focus on assigning labels to nodes with high confidence levels, this method selects pseudo-labels for nodes with low confidence levels. As nodes with low confidence levels are typically difficult to classify and less influential in the predicted outcomes, this method prevents the model from being biased towards easily identifiable nodes. Additionally, this method proactively guards against data distribution shifts by assigning pseudo-labels to nodes whose local structure and features differ significantly from their predicted classes. By doing so, this method ensures that the model is trained with a broader range of unsupervised nodes, thereby improving its ability to adapt to shifting data distributions. Experimentally demonstrated on multiple node classification tasks, this method outperforms conventional pseudo-labeling techniques and graph neural networks.

Our research introduces PatchNet, a lightweight convolutional neural network
designed for efficient processing of spatiotemporal data. By replacing MobileNetV2
components with patch-based operations, we create a more computationally
efficient model. The resulting network achieves superior performance while requiring
minimal memory and computation compared to MobileNetV2 and other modern backbones.
Notably, PatchNet surpasses MobileNetV2 in performance on popular object detection
benchmarks such as COCO and Kinetics-YOLO, with an impressive gain of over 5% in
mAP and over 30% in accuracy, respectively, at a comparable computational cost.

A review of recent findings on multi-point distributions in the TASEP model is presented. The TASEP model, especially in discrete time, has become a key area of study within probability theory. The review begins by highlighting how taking multiple observations into account can lead to significantly higher accuracy when estimating key statistical measures. It then explores how initial conditions influence the multi-point distribution in a discrete time TASEP and shows that this distribution becomes increasingly diverse as time progresses. Next, the review focuses on stationary solutions to the TASEP model. It presents both exact calculations of multi-point distributions for certain special cases and discusses the feasibility of computing such distributions for more general cases. Lastly, the review touches upon how taking multiple observations can be applied to estimate key statistical measures called correlation functions within the TASEP model.

This study investigates the optimization of data transfer rate in a SWIPT-enabled wireless communication network with dynamic changes in user demand and available energy. To enhance energy efficiency, a generalized antenna-switching technique is used to split each transmitter into multiple antennas, allowing simultaneous data transfer to multiple users and energy harvesting from each antenna. Through mathematical analysis, the theoretical limits of energy efficiency and information transfer rate are determined. Further, a practical algorithm based on fractional programming is developed to optimize the network and proven to achieve optimal performance in scenarios with low dynamic demand. Additionally, a novel algorithm is proposed for optimizing the network when there is significant dynamic demand. This algorithm is composed of multiple stages: first, the achievable rate and energy harvest are calculated for each user, then an iterative process is used to optimize the network, and finally, a QoS-based algorithm is used to optimize the antenna configuration. Simulation results show that this algorithm can efficiently optimize the network and that using GAST outperforms traditional approaches in terms of energy efficiency.

We've developed a general approach to perturbation theory for SU(N) fermions using a fermionic bare-particle language. For SU(N) color symmetry, we've successfully derived an analytical expression for the free energy of a fermion gas to second-order in the coupling constant, with our method producing results that differ from standard second-order approaches. Our approach allows us to extend perturbation theory to any order, with the formula consisting of a sum of fermion interactions. Our method can be applied to any number of fermions and colors by generalizing the Fermi-Feynman trick. Our technique also facilitates the derivation of the SU(N) free energy to any specified order without a bosonization of the fermions. Our method may have applications in studying exotic quark matter and other SU(N) fermion systems.

In optomechanics, the quantum treatment is often replaced by classical methods when occupation numbers are substantial. This paper bridges the gap between the quantum and classical approaches by using a finite-dimensional quantum simulation. It employs two distinct strategies: one based on the truncated Weyl-Witter equation and another utilizing a quantum Monte Carlo method. These methods were applied to analyze single-photon dynamics, combining non-linear cavity field interactions with a wide range of occupational probabilities for the mechanical oscillator. The simulation results matched exactly with those obtained from a continuous complex-valued equation that incorporates cavity field phase information, highlighting the importance of phase for optimizing optomechanical interactions. Furthermore, the study identified the minimum required occupation number for the mechanical oscillator to utilize quasi-classical conditions.

On the nonnegative axis, a continuous linear system that weighs functions continuously is established based on a generalized sextic Freud weight. This new weight is expressed as a sixth power of a function that includes x to the fifth, multiplied by the square root of a semicircle polynomial, and a constant factor. The system induced by this weighted norm shares many of the same properties with the system induced by the generalized Airy weight, yet differs from it. Notably, it possesses a wider set of functions it can support. A broader set of functions is also defined, which includes polynomials, yet exceeds the set supported by the generalized Airy weight. The name "generalized sextic Freud" weight arises from a connection to the sextic Freud weight and a constant factor, which is the thteenth root of a special constant. The paper concludes by exploring potential future research into orthogonal polynomials related to hypergeometric functions.

A basic model of a robot following a wall is developed in this paper to study how its sensing capabilities impact its navigation. The sensor's field of view and range are the key factors being investigated, as they influence the robot's movement along the wall. It's found that, unlike previously claimed, the robot's trajectory can vary significantly based on these sensing factors. Consequently, a more accurate model of the robot is proposed, which better captures its behavior and provides insights into the optimal control strategies for successful wall-following navigation.

This article focuses on the perturbative continuum perturbative algebraic quantum field theory, particularly irreducible, subalgebras defined on various Cauchy surfaces. It investigates the theory's subalgebras and the relations between them. Additionally, it considers the reconstruction of a quantum field theory from its perturbative perturbative form.

The increasing use of robotic surgeries has led to the advancement of "smoke" detection via camera observation. Unlike conventional methods which rely on explicit image fusion or simultaneous training of smoke and non-smoke categories, our proposed dual learning approach trains two separate models, one optimized for smoke images and another for non-smoke images. However, our preliminary evaluation showed that dual learning alone lacked sufficient correlation for effective cross-category training. Therefore, to improve the classification of smoke and non-smoke images, we integrated dual learning with a dual asymmetrical supervision method. Specifically, I defined smoke images as high-intensity visual data and non-smoke images as low-intensity visual data. Based on this intensity difference, I developed a dual asymmetrical method that calculates the loss of one category using the other model's predictions. As a result, the dual learning approach was capable of not only enhancing the discrimination between smoke and non-smoke images, but also reducing training time and data requirements. My research demonstrated that the integrated model achieved better accuracy in smoke and non-smoke image classification compared to a baseline model trained simultaneously on smoke and non-smoke images. We introduce a set of robust molecular gate methods, incorporating a broad
frequency range with the potential to significantly increase entanglement across
ion chains. Unlike traditional gate methods, our design doesn't rely on a
narrow frequency margin, instead utilizing a strategy that accounts for and
compensates for secondary laser beams. This approach enables the creation of
robust gates capable of handling a substantial amount of frequency
misalignment, particularly beneficial in large-scale ion computers where precise
frequency control may not be feasible. Utilizing Monte Carlo simulations, our
research examines the performance of robust Molmer-Sorensen gates in both excited
and ground states, identifying a critical threshold for robust gate operation across
ion chains.

The equilibrium structure of the perovskite LaBO$_3$ with various A cations (Ca, Sr, Ba) was investigated through ab-initio calculations. These studies focused on the effects of ion size, bond lengths, and filler A cation on the movement of B cations within the lattice. Generally, increasing the size of the A cation leads to increased off-centering of the B cation. Bond lengths primarily influence the displacement of the B cation along the perpendicular axis. Additionally, the equilibrium structure of LaBO$_3$ with different A cations was examined under the pressure of 10 GPa, revealing distinct behavior for each filler.

Multivariate Gaussian processes form the basis of several machine learning models, including regression, classification, and interpolation, particularly suitable for large-scale data. They, however, fail to capture dependencies between individual processes in a predictive framework. Such dependencies can be modeled using a graphical representation known as multivariate Gaussian graphical models. Cross-covariance matrices, often estimated with limited accuracy in real-world applications, are crucial to determining the structure of these models. We therefore developed a novel sparse multivariate Gaussian graphical model based on covariance estimation. By incorporating a sparsity-inducing regularizer, this model is able to determine both dependent and independent processes, particularly useful in predicting multiple processes with varying degrees of correlation. The model's efficacy was validated through numerical experiments on synthetic and real-world data.

The applications of deep quantum neural networks are numerous but their practical use is hindered by their significant scaling of computational resources to the number of qubits. This limitation makes them unsuitable for processing large molecular systems unless we find ways to reduce the required resources or more efficiently utilize available ones. One potential approach is using recurrent quantum circuits, which hold promise by reducing the scaling to the square root of the number of qubits, although the expense is still higher than what we find in classical recurrent neural networks. In this study, we found that replacing quantum neural networks with their parametric quantum circuit learning involves a similar scaling improvement, and we propose a method to further minimize the required resources by applying a diagonal basis transformation. This improvement allows us to compute the ground state of larger molecular systems more efficiently using quantum neural networks. In our experiments, we found that the diagonal basis transformation leads to a significant reduction of the required gate count, and for some cases, the scaling improves to a lower power of the number of qubits, more in line with what we see in classical recurrent neural networks. Additionally, we found that quantum neural networks are capable of accurately calculating the ground state of complex molecular systems such as beryllium hydride and hydrogen cyanide.

The Gr\"obner basis algorithm is one of the most versatile methods for resolving polynomial systems, but its worst-case efficiency makes it uncompetitive. Researchers have recently discovered that, on average, the algorithm converges rapidly, specifically with the same speed of geometrically decreasing errors seen in modern optimization techniques such as gradient descent. In fact, a more efficient variant known as the Strassen algorithm achieves comparable average-case performance for solving polynomial systems. Both of these methods fall under generalized Chebyshev interpolation, an area of study that our work significantly advances by proving the algorithmic and theoretical foundations of this technique, further refining it with significantly simpler proofs, and demonstrating its practical efficacy through multiple high-profile polynomial system solving examples. Additionally, our work generalizes Chebyshev interpolation in an innovative way, opening up potential applications in various fields such as numerical analysis and optimization techniques.

Moir\'e superlattices created by twisting two monolayers of different semiconductors together exhibit unique electronic properties that are not found in standard material science. For example, interlayer excitons, which consist of electrons and holes located in separate layers, can be stabilized through this moir\'e superlattice and exhibit long-lived emission when they recombine. In theory, this emission can be modified by applying an electric field that stretches one layer relative to the other, thus either increasing or decreasing the distance between electrons and holes. A theoretical model has been developed to study how this stretching affects the binding energy of interlayer excitons and their associated emission spectra. The results show that a significant change in the binding energy can occur when this stretching is on the order of 1%, and that the interlayer exciton emission may even dominate the emission spectra under certain conditions. In fact, this emission could potentially be thousands of times stronger than emissions caused by electrons and holes located within the same layer.

This study investigates adaptive methods for positioning and tracking a mobile entity. We propose an adaptive algorithm that recalculates the parameters of a probabilistic data association algorithm based on real-time measurement data. We demonstrate the benefits of this approach by adapting it to a problem involving a mobile agent that relies on spatio-temporal data from sensors such as dead reckoning, inertial sensors, and time-related metrics. This is a difficult positioning problem due to errors that accumulate rapidly and create complex dynamics. We demonstrate the adaptive PDA method's superiority to conventional solutions that utilize constant parameters or simplified models, such as a particle filter using a constant velocity model, through simulation-based comparison and evaluation. Specifically, our results show that the adaptive PDA method leads to a significant reduction of position error by as much as 85% and trajectory similarity improvement of up to 90%, particularly in dynamic environments, compared to these alternative approaches.

ATLAS has cooperated with CMS to investigate the helicity properties of boson production using data collected at 13 TeV, analyzing 2015 and 2016 data with a combined total of 139 fb^-1 of luminosity. The study utilized simulations of polarized boson creation to determine expected helicity distributions, and then compared these with actual measurements to validate predictions from the Standard Model. It measured the co-polarization states of W+ and W- bosons and the Z boson, finding joint helicity fractions that aligned with, but were slightly greater than, Standard Model forecasts for right-handed and transversely polarized states. Conversely, the joint helicity fractions for left-handed and longitudinal transversely polarized states showed smaller discrepancies. The joint helicity fractions for W and Z bosons demonstrated consistency with, but did not verify, Standard Model predictions. The joint helicity fractions for co-polarized W bosons revealed a slight excess, around 5%, in comparison to Standard Model predictions, while the joint helicity fractions for the Z boson revealed no notable deviation from Standard Model predictions. The joint helicity fractions for co-polarized W+ and W- bosons, as well as the Z boson, also demonstrated consistency with Standard Model predictions based on the most up-to-date results from other studies, showing the preference for additional new physics in boson production.
