Our research delves into the underlying geometry of genomic data obtained from single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq). We observed that categorization of scRNA-seq data in lower-dimensional product space results in substantially enhanced performance, offering improvements of of approximately 50% to 100% in comparison to Euclidean-based methods. Furthermore, such enhanced rankings are transferable to target prediction tasks. We identified that these favorable outcomes are largely attributed to the incorporation of semantic information present in the combined annotation of cells. Notably, in product space, neighboring data points exhibit increased correlation in annotated information. This phenomenon allows for the development of more effective classification models, as the likelihood of simultaneous presence of multiple annotations within a local region increases with the dimensionality of the product space. Building upon this insight, we propose a novel clustering algorithm (Semantics-Based Embedding Clustering, or RUBI-ABC) that harnesses the proximity of annotated data points in product space. In comparison to alternative methods, RUBI-ABC demonstrates significantly improved clustering results across multiple datasets.

Our investigation into the scattering of stars by a supermassive black hole reveals that the mass function of stars significantly impacts the outcome, and that using a delta-function mass distribution overcounts the number of stars scattered. Utilizing analytical solutions for non-interacting stars with unique orbital energies, we derive formulas for minimizing scattering losses, and validate our findings through cometary encounters. For the first time, we provide a comprehensive account of all relevant physical phenomena of stars encountering a supermassive black hole, and propose a novel statistical method, based on phase-space density, for comparing the mass distributions of stars within a specific radial space near a supermassive black hole. This method can be used to compare observed mass functions with theoretical predictions in various astronomical environments, such as globular clusters, dwarf galaxies, and galaxy cores.

This presentation focuses on stochastic Model Predictive Control applied to uncertain systems, highlighting that uncertainty impacts its effectiveness, often necessitating smaller control signals than would be ideal in a perfectly known environment. A crucial challenge involves determining a valid convex approximation of the stochastic MPC problem, which becomes acute when model uncertainty is significant. Convex approximations can lead to suboptimal performance but offer a solution when other methods fail. This discussion explores the implementation of an MPC strategy on a quadrotor navigating through a virtual environment.

This research explores compressive ICA (Independent Component Analysis) algorithms that reduce the dimensionality of mixed signals through subsampling and component-wise measurement. We introduce two new compressive ICA algorithms - ComprIca1 and ComprIca2 - that incorporate an orthogonal less-than-or-equal-to equal-to unitary transformation. Our findings reveal the performance of these algorithms in various scenarios. To evaluate their effectiveness, we measured their ability to recover sources from mixed signals under different subsampling rates and spam levels. Our numerical experiments demonstrate that ComprIca2 surpasses ComprIca1 and traditional ICA methods like FastICA and JADE in most cases. Interestingly, ComprIca2 even outperforms the original ICA algorithms with ideal subsampling and spam levels. Our study showcases the memory efficiency of our compressive ICA algorithms, which requires fewer measurements and memory accesses than vector quantization-based ComprICA and the original ICA methods.

The paper explores the dynamics of the asymmetric noisy voter model with two types of species, examining how species interact and outcome patterns emerge. Through analysis and numerical investigations, we identify fixed points, transient coexistence, periodic and complex pattern formations. The existence of a unique stationary distribution in the homogeneous noisy voter model sets a foundation for our research. Further insights into the model's behavior are gained through a system that dynamically changes species probabilities over time, influencing how species compete and outcomes unfold.

This article investigates von Neumann algebras generated by bounded functions on the set of possible configurations for a physical system with a finite number of particles, derived from the C*-algebra associated with the system's Hilbert space. A specific segment of this von Neumann algebra, known as the 'locally confined' segment, is analyzed, which corresponds to functions defined over smaller sub-systems. A complete characterization of the locally confined von Neumann algebras arising from ground states is achieved, when the system exhibits frustration-free behavior. The proof relies on a recently introduced concept in [arXiv:1802.04521]. The study also shows that these characterizations are not applicable when the system has interactions with an infinite number of particles, which is exemplified using the Jonsson algebra as an example.

The ability of a system to stay entangled even when subjected to heat is enhanced by introducing a coordinated feedback loop that tracks the temperature. To investigate this enhancement, we study an experiment involving cavities connected to two sets of moving mirrors, with the movement of the mirrors orchestrated by two lasers whose phases are linked in a coordinated feedback loop. We find that the entanglement between the cavities is robust against heat when the coordinated feedback loop is operating, and that this resistance to heat is increased by adjusting the speed at which the lasers' phases change to match the frequency of the heat process. We further demonstrate that the entanglement can be maintained for an extended period by adjusting this adjustment to match the frequency of the heat process and then turning on an additional cooling mechanism. (Phys. Rev. A 97, 022504, 2008).

One-loop triple-collinear splitting operators for massless gluons have been
computed within QCD to allow the derivation of subtraction terms required for
accurate next-to-next-to-leading order perturbative QCD calculations. The
derived splitting operators will facilitate the development of an effective
theory for multiple small momentum scales, enabling the computation of
cross-sections with an arbitrary number of final-state particles at NNLO.

Greenberg's strong approximation conjecture has been influenced by various refinements, including ones made by Serre and Nekovar. Our contribution offers a refined version that addresses an aspect of this influence for rings with a $p$-group as its $p$-primary part, where Greenberg's original hypothesis is confirmed under specific conditions for such rings having only one $p$-component. When this ring is further defined as a local one, our result expands upon an earlier finding by Nekovar, and in the case where the ring has only one $p$-component, our statement aligns with a conjecture proposed by Haroski and Nekovar.

Sundials found across Indonesia's diverse regions, reflecting various cultures and histories, await a deeper understanding. As a crucial archaeological find, sundials need to be documented thoroughly, encompassing detailed description, measurement, and geographic mapping. To support and facilitate this process, a citizen science initiative can be leveraged. By engaging the general public, citizen science enables the gathering of essential information, including photographs, which can then be analyzed together with existing data to create a comprehensive database. This study proposes a combined approach of top-down and bottom-up methods to collect sundial information, involving not only crowd-sourcing, but also official institutions and the general public as well. Furthermore, a framework for sustainable sundial documentation is presented, ensuring long-term access to the collected data.

In a 2D DED-based cellular network, users inside a circularly symmetric, bounded area around each antenna can receive data and energy from that antenna. A TFIET (Two-Fiber Information Exchange and Transfer) scheme enables data and energy transfer between users within a fiber-based area by converting it into analog signals. A recent study extended TFIET to be used in a DED-based cellular network. This paper develops an optimal power allocation strategy to maximize the energy efficiency of the extended TFIET in a DED-based cellular network. The power allocation strategy is based on a convex optimization that considers the TFIET schedule, user locations, and the need for equal treatment in the TFIET process. The optimization is solved by a successive convex optimization algorithm and leads to equal energy efficiency for users inside a bounded area around each antenna. The equal power allocation strategy leads to equal data transfer rates for these users, which is confirmed analytically. Additionally, it is shown that equal power allocation reduces the TFIET schedule complexity and enables equal data transfer rates per unit energy for users on the boundary of the bounded area. The results show that equal power allocation improves energy efficiency and enables better use of the TFIET schedule in a DED-based cellular network.

The COVID-19 pandemic led to a significant increase in remote work, leading to a high demand for automated experimental setups that can be easily accessed and controlled remotely.  This paper presents an innovative, fully-automated system designed for non-technical personnel to set up, run experiments remotely, and collect and process data in real-time, streamlining the process with remote oversight by experts.  The developed platform integrates high-performance computing, remote control of equipment, and efficient data management, enabling experiments that need to run for extended periods without interruption.  Its experimental validation consisted of an assessment of the system's capabilities in conducting radio frequency signal strength measurements.

We examine the partial linear algebra of graphs. Specifically, we investigate the partial linear algebra of undirected bipartite graphs, and our analysis sheds new light on Asser's conjecture regarding the class of spectra. By synthesizing linear algebra techniques with combinatorial principles, we obtain both upper and lower limits on the rank of the combinatorial sum of two bipartite graphs. Our results are further encapsulated in an inequality, the Combinatorial Cauchy Intersection Lemma, and we show that it leads to both conservative estimates of rank and precise rank calculations in various instances. Ultimately, we demonstrate that Asser's conjecture remains unresolved even within the realm of undirected bipartite graphs.

To plan the construction of a custom electrostatic phase plate with optimal performance for observing ice nucleation at the individual ice crystal level, a study was conducted to assess the impact of design choices on electron probe characteristics.  A suitable design was identified for a phase plate that maintains the ice crystal's hexagonal symmetry while creating multiple ice-like tubes, and the results of this investigation will guide the phase plate's manufacture to achieve the desired outcome.

Automated systems that rely on quantum computation must comply with specific rules governing quantum circuits, circuit evolution, and observation measurements. These mechanisms of computation are fundamentally distinct from one another, each with unique properties. Despite being incompatible, we can merge them into a unified framework of computation. This merged framework enables us to derive a formal structure consisting of orthogonal states, an algebra of linear operators, and an execution model that mimics circuit evolution and observation measurements. This structure is akin to that of quantum computation, but we'll show it has inherent flaws that make it incompatible with quantum computation. Conversely, we can prove that a particular type of computation in this merged framework has properties analogous to those of probabilistic computation.

We investigate the number of unique positions visited in a discrete, d-dimensional random walk over a bounded cube within a metric space, showing that this count varies significantly between d and d+1 dimensions. Specifically, while the former tends towards d times the surface area of the cube as the number of steps n grows, the latter exhibits logarithmic growth. By applying these findings to the simplest cases (d=1 and d=2), we derive new insights into Polya's random walk and Rumsfeld's unknown unknowns.

Recently proposed wormhole solutions exhibit similarities to certain spacetimes, including those of polymer black holes and cosmological vacua. We explore whether the differences between these spacetimes justify their categorization as distinct solutions. Employing the spherically symmetric Einstein-Hilbert action with a non-polynomial potential, we investigate various aspects, such as caustic formation, energy conditions, and boundary layer thickness. Our analysis indicates that, despite caustic formation and caustic-free regimes, differences in boundary layer thicknesses and energy conditions exist for all regimes, distinguishing polymer black holes from wormholes.

The charge and heat transport within doped graphene have been studied theoretically in the context of weak electron-electron interactions. An underlying theory based on the Dirac equation with a Coulomb interaction is used and developed into a hydrodynamic model. The specific heat and transport coefficients of this model were then calculated and analyzed in terms of the graphene sheet size and doping levels. These properties were found to be strongly affected by a thermal correction to the quasiparticle velocity, which was derived from the underlying many-body theory. The results showed that this correction could either increase or decrease quasiparticle scattering rates, thereby deviating from the standard Fermi velocity and conventional behavior. In particular, the specific heat was observed to exhibit a size-dependent transition between a quadratic temperature dependence and a linear temperature dependence, while the transport coefficients displayed nonintuitive velocity dependence. The numerical analysis revealed that this phenomenon could potentially be detectable in graphene samples up to 100nm in size. The study concluded with an exploration of the impact of boundary conditions on quasiparticle scattering rates and the associated graphene size.

Recent advances in text-to-speech research have led to the development of a method that synthesizes more expressive and natural voice by incorporating speech paralingual characteristics, such as speech rate, loudness, and speech spectral slope. This characteristic can be learned from large datasets of speaking voices and allows for a more detailed representation of human vocal characteristics. However, existing studies often rely on speech categorization databases, which are limited in their ability to capture the full range of human vocal expressions. This research presents MaskedSpeech, an unsupervised data augmentation method capable of generating diverse vocal expressions by masking certain speech features. By applying this method to a large speech dataset, we can create richer and more varied speech phenomena, ultimately enhancing the accuracy and effectiveness of voice synthesis systems. Experimental results indicate that MaskedSpeech significantly surpasses existing methods in automatically identifying speech characteristics. Furthermore, when integrated with a voice transformer model, it leads to a substantial improvement in the synthesis quality of human-like paralingual characteristics.

Variable selection is a fundamental task in modeling. We have developed a novel approach to enhance the stability of variables in existing models through subtle modifications. The proposed method iteratively utilizes a Bayesian framework to maintain the original model's posterior uncertainties while introducing a small, randomized perturbation to select additional variables. By employing a sparse Gaussian priors for coefficient vectors, our approach effectively controls the number of significant variables while ensuring the retention of the original model's posterior uncertainties, thus enhancing variable selection stability. We have tested our approach on 100 real-world datasets and found that it surpasses 15 established variable selection methods in terms of predictive accuracy, often with fewer selected variables.

Deep Neural Networks are susceptible to attacks that exploit their reliance on data, particularly data that can be manipulated by attackers. Despite extensive research on generating adversarial examples, a specific type of attack - the Man-in-the-Middle attack, which involves intercepting data, is under-researched. In this research, we explore the feasibility of completing incomplete data received by users, with the aim of misleading them with altered content. Our novel approach to completing data involves creating a data representation space using the Variational Autoencoder, which allows us to detect when data is tampered with and accurately predict the original input. Our experiments on image classification, particularly with MNIST and CIFAR10, indicate that our method effectively mitigates Man-in-the-Middle attacks, outperforming existing defenses in the process.

Climate change conspiracy beliefs are being rapidly disseminated across social media platforms. Our analysis reveals that right-wing populists are consistently spreading conspiracy theories related to climate change, often using the same messaging tactics repeatedly. In contrast, mainstream groups occasionally circulate such beliefs, but predominantly promote counter-narratives. Conversely, left-wing extremists, although infrequent in their climate-related conspiracy theory dissemination, tend to promote more violent and extremist forms of such beliefs. A significant proportion of online conspiracy theory-related content originates from a distinct group of individuals who consistently promote such narratives.

Dark matter models involving a low-energy portal have the potential to yield visible signs such as scattering or lepton production if dark matter interacts with particles of similar mass. If no indication of this type of interaction is detected, it does not rule out the validity of such a model as it may simply imply that dark matter has a significantly larger mass than the intermediate state particle. Consequently, we look for signs of the intermediate state particle itself, specifically its decay into the dark matter state and a photon. The resulting process has a characteristic distribution g-vertex and can potentially be identified through observations of final states containing photons and large momentum transfers. Existing experiments have the capability to search for this process and can verify the standard model's predictions by examining the photon energy and momentum transfer in their data.

Building upon earlier work, Ettinger and Yan established that for a triangulated category with a weakly holomorphic enhancement, Serre duality holds if and only if a certain condition is met - namely, that the category exhibits Exn-weakly flat deformation over a field that has only two elements. Subsequently, in the published version of the work, Ettinger and Yan made further contributions, including proving that for any Exn-weakly flat deformation in a two-element field, Birkenake's decomposition holds, and consequently, Serre duality exists. In response to questions posed by Paul Balakrishnan and Martin Grandjean, it is now being investigated whether similar decompositions of Birkenake's type might exist within certain subcategories of the two-element field's Exn-weakly flat deformation. Specifically, this research focuses on whether and how decompositions of this nature might arise within the subcategory of g-filtered objects within Exn-weakly flat deformation. In order to address this question, a series of new theorems and corollaries are being introduced, the primary being that for g-filtered objects within Exn-weakly flat deformation, Serre duality exists provided that Exn-weakly flat deformation is known to be G-demitopic over a two-element field, with the condition that G is compatible with the notion of g-filtered objects. This study provides the first nationwide evaluation of the returns on investment to different fields of study in Norway. The findings are compared to those of Denmark, where a similar assessment has been conducted since 2007. The data show significant disparities in the earnings potential of various fields of study between Norway and Denmark. For example, students pursuing mathematics or computer science in Norway can expect lower earnings than those in statistics or biological science, whereas the opposite is true in Denmark. The differences between the two countries suggest that market forces may not always accurately reflect the earnings potential of various fields of study. As a result, state subsidies for certain programs may not be justified and could be reevaluated.

A high-intensity $B$-meson factory with a super $J/ho$ resonance line offers an exceptional opportunity to explore new research possibilities in particle physics. Equipped with advanced particle detectors, this facility would offer an extensive detection range for a broad spectrum of $B$-meson decays, including those involving the $J/ho$ intermediate state. Some of the promising areas of study that this factory would enable include in-depth analyses of $B$-meson structure, precise $cp$-violating processes, rare $B$-meson decays, and a detailed understanding of the $J/ho$ resonance line, all while offering a substantial detection range for a wide variety of $B$-meson decay types.
