Our study employs three-dimensional SPH simulations to analyze the accretion
processes in hierarchical triple systems. The study's setup involved pairing a
massive binary with a solo star or a binary with half the mass, surrounded by
an accretion disk, against which it interacted in a series of simulations. The
massive binary maintained its identity and disc mass decreased due to the
star's interaction, whereas against a less massive binary, the trio's interaction
resulted in the formation of a common envelope. In contrast, against a solo star,
the star's accretion disk increased in mass, potentially leading to the merger
of the star with the binary, aided by the disk's disruption of the binary's orbit
and subsequent mass exchange. Interestingly, against a solo star, the binary's accretion
behaved similarly to a single star of equivalent mass, whereas against a more
massive binary, it deviated from such expectations, instead exhibiting less accretion
than a single star. The study offers implications for the understanding of stellar
triple systems in the context of stellar evolution.

The behavior of bi-symmetric cosmological models under general relativity is examined in this research. We start by looking at the general characteristics of these models, then derive equations that explain how matter affects the structure of the universe over time. We solve these equations using a technique that involves approximating small deviations, and find solutions for specific cases using special assumptions. The validity of these solutions is confirmed through analytical calculations. We conclude by exploring the physical implications of our findings.

We modify the piecewise constant Mumford-Shah model to enhance the segmentation of degraded images. Our new approach introduces a weighted term that prioritizes regions with sharper boundaries in the image, thereby improving overall segmentation accuracy. A demixing technique is then employed to restore the segmented pieces, using the smoothed level sets as guides to optimize the segmentation process. A stable algorithm is developed to iteratively optimize both the segmentation and the restoration steps. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our method in improving segmentations of corrupted images, particularly those with distinct and clear boundaries.

The maximum velocity of dark matter particles, associated with ultra-light particles, can be inferred through observations of galaxy rotation curves. This velocity serves as a direct consequence of the particle's mass and a fundamental constant, representing the quantum gravitational interaction. Consequently, constraints can be imposed on the particle's mass and the constant in question. Within the framework of wave-particle interactions, our analysis reveals that the particle's mass is constrained below the Planck mass, with a precision of better than one part in a hundred million. This finding, however, raises an issue of consistency with the current understanding of quantum gravity. Alternatively, our data do not rule out the possibility that dark matter consists mainly of particles with masses ranging from microelectronvolts to hundredth of a microelectronvolt. Such particles would require coupling strengths of Planck-scale magnitude, thereby invalidating the conventional description of quantum gravity.

Neuromorphic computing holds promise for delivering unprecedented performance gains through on-chip learning of spiking neural networks.  In contrast to conventional learning techniques, which rely on synchronizing global updates with external data, on-chip learning enables simultaneous computation of gradient updates and weight updates within the hardware.  By leveraging local event-driven computations, this approach enables true real-time learning.  Within this framework, we develop novel spike-driven learning algorithms for adding new neurons and synapses during online training.  To demonstrate the feasibility of on-chip learning, we constructed a 128-neuron spiking circuit on a 64-tane NeuronCortex chip and successfully trained it to classify binary data at 1MS/s through spontaneous activity.  Additionally, we trained the same circuit to learn a more complex data stream at 1MS/s after initially tuning it with 10ms presentations of a related template signal.  Both training protocols relied on common random axes for data and template vectors.  Our results show that the trained circuit can discriminate spiking patterns at frequencies far exceeding hardware's own event frequency, up to 125.86 KHz.

Images taken by the Euipse VUV imaging spectrometer on board the NOX solar orbiter observed a major geomagnetic storm on May 6, 2022, with unprecedented clarity in the wavelength range of 120-140 Angstroms. The storm's image showed an incredible symmetry similar to that of an egg or a prolate ellipse with alternating bright and dark stripes. The extreme brightness reached as high as 20 times the typical value in the storm's center, with its shape changing rapidly into a more stable form over a duration of about 10 minutes. The initial splitting of the storm's image into two distinct parts was followed by their merger into a single, more stable shape. The speed at which the storm's shape changed can be related to the speed of sound in the solar atmosphere, with the observed pattern believed to be a type of oscillation known as a sausage mode. The rapid change in the storm's shape over a short distance is thought to be caused by a small and intense source of the storm, with its size estimated to be less than 10,000 km, comparable to the size of a planetary scale wave. The extreme brightness of the storm, however, supports the theory of a highly intense and compact source, possibly related to a type of solar flare known as a mini-flare, producing an extraordinary level of energy of about 10 to the power of 24 ergs in a brief period of time.

We've revised the design of a magnetically-optical trap (MOT) used to capture a Bose-Einstein condensate, incorporating planar integration to compactify the design while enhancing its cooling capabilities. A comparative analysis between this new design and conventional setups has shown that planar integration improves trapping efficiency by as much as 80% when compared to a trap of equivalent size. To validate our design, we performed theoretical calculations of the trap's cooling capacity using a classical statistical model and found that this new design can capture up to 120% more atoms compared to a trap of the same size. Additionally, we've measured and experimentally verified the trap's cooling capacity and found it to be in perfect agreement with our theoretical predictions.

The powerful jets emanating from supermassive black holes like Sgr A* and M87* come as a surprise, given their relatively low energy output. This discrepancy may be resolved if these black holes are surrounded by a dynamic disk of accretion, with variations in the jet's brightness attributed to changes in the disk's structure and how it interacts with the black hole. Such a scenario would result in a pattern of correlated movement between the jet's brightness and its polarization properties, which has been observed with Sgr A*. Furthermore, variations in the disk's behavior could potentially produce recurring patterns, or oscillations, in the jet's brightness and polarization. These oscillations may be linked to the phenomenon of "states changes" commonly observed in black holes and neutron stars.

The work explores how the motion of a neutral atom interacting with a mirror and photons differs from standard descriptions. Unlike typical models, the atom is not simply tied to the photons, but rather its motion is influenced by the reflection at the mirror and resulting forces. This leads to the atom emitting photons that are then reflected, but the emitted photons no longer form a collimated beam due to the atom's motion, and instead the photons become collimated in a specific direction relative to the atom's motion. This effect is analogous to the observation of collimated light emitted by neutrons when moving through a crystal lattice.

A century ago, the presence of supernovae was hypothesized by a Russian astronomer. For the past eight decades, there has been no documented evidence of such an occurrence. A nearby and a relatively young massive cluster, known as Westerlund 2, is believed to follow the typical path of a massive star formation. Research on this cluster has identified eight massive-star ejections, five of which are thought to have undergone a supernova. By studying the cluster's remaining stellar members, it's estimated that up to 30% of massive stars in this cluster have either exploded as supernovae or lost a significant amount of mass. This finding is consistent with previous studies on a nearby star cluster, known as the Carina Nebula Cluster. Our study, however, suggests that the likelihood of detecting a massive-star supernova in a young cluster may be lower than previously thought. By comparing the cluster's properties to a nearby star cluster, known as the Quintuplet Cluster at the center of our galaxy, it's suggested that Westerlund 2 is unlikely to be the source of a recently discovered extreme runaway star, NLAC 111670.

We've established the existence of minimal elements in a variational problem with a strong and continuous objective function and a metric space with a continuous and weakly-continuous perturbation function. This result is based on the minimax principle and a topological degree theorem from the degree theory of set-valued mappings. We've also demonstrated that the existence of minimal elements in this problem is equivalent to the existence of an global minimizer in a related problem after applying a compactification transformation to the original problem. We've used this result to prove the existence of minimal elements in problems involving the principal eigenvalue of PDEs under various boundary conditions, as well as to prove the existence of an efficient policy in stochastic single-server and continuous-state discrete-service queueing models.

Degraded document images can be optimized using Deep Learning-based non-rigid image
embedding methods. However, these methods require pre-trained image enhancers and
text recognizers. In this research, we integrate a state-of-the-art text recognizer with
Generative Adversarial Networks (GAN) to improve the quality of degraded document images.
The project, called RIGAN, includes efficient and cost-effective approaches to
recursively refine image features and generate text. We evaluate RIGAN by hand-writing
the text portion of multiple datasets, including SVHN-MNIST, EMNIST, and 64K custom
handwritten digits. The experiment results demonstrate that RIGAN surpasses competing
methods in generating accurate and legible text from degraded images, especially for
handwritten digits. The project's code and pre-trained models are freely accessible on
https://github.com/alexarchd/edited-image-generation.

This research focuses on developing an Information Extraction system for identification cards, specifically ID and driver's licenses, with an aim to improve extraction efficiency. We investigated how Deep Learning methods could be utilized in this context. A key consideration was the conservation of company and national identification number extraction fields, as these often employ diverse, complex fonts not easily processable by computers. To tackle this challenge, we employed an NLP approach, incorporating a pre-trained Language Model, to enhance our model's performance and achieve higher extraction accuracy. Building on this foundation, we constructed a custom NN architecture, combining an attention-based encoder-decoder model, to effectively extract text from images, even when the font is unfamiliar. This two-part approach, an NLP feature extractor and a Deep Learning-based text extractor, enabled our model to accurately extract citizenship and identification numbers, as well as enhance overall extraction efficiency. We conducted a comprehensive comparison of this hybrid method with other leading ID extraction techniques and found it yielded superior results. Additionally, we developed a mobile application to facilitate easy identification of ID cards using your device's camera, thus simplifying the process for both basic and advanced users. This work was fully implemented as an open-source project on GitHub. We also presented our findings at the Student Research Forum in ICML 2021.

This study proposes an adaptive channel estimation method that utilizes memory in its algorithmic model. The method leverages a learning algorithm within the mobile device to predict channel conditions by taking past measurements into account, thereby enhancing channel estimation accuracy across various scenarios, including stationary and mobile scenarios. The study examines and compares the performance of this method with conventional channel estimation methods that rely on the assumption of static or slowly-changing channels, and finds that the method offers improved estimation accuracy in high-mobility scenarios when synthetically simulated. The study also reveals that certain deep learning algorithms can serve as efficient channel estimators when their adaptive nature is properly harnessed.

We utilize a Bayesian algorithm and Markov chain Monte Carlo simulations to enhance low-resolution astronomical images, specifically applying it to a case study of the ALMA antenna at 4830 meters above sea level in Chile. The method successfully restores camera images of the sky to high spatial resolution, accurately representing the observed variability of the atmosphere at high altitudes. The top-performing model, evaluated by the widely-used Valliappan index, achieved a significant improvement of 93% with only 50 iterations. The resulting restored images are applicable to other astronomical instruments, offering a valuable enhancement of images taken under unstable atmospheric conditions.

We suggest an alternative to traditional supervised learning techniques, where a neural network is trained to classify inputs by minimizing the difference between the input's projection onto a predefined data manifold and the target class's representation on that manifold. This novel approach is based on a novel optimization algorithm and a new method for generating synthetic data. Conventional supervised learning techniques can struggle with overfitting, which is often addressed by increasing the dataset size or the model's complexity. In contrast, our method directly optimizes the target class's representation and incorporates an automatic dataset enlargement mechanism to prevent overfitting by generating synthetic counterexamples for incorrect classes during training.

In 2018, the ECFA Early Career Researchers' panel initiated its operations, aimed at representing and addressing the concerns of ECFA members in an early stage of their careers. This year, the panel organized a series of online workshops focused on research and project management skills essential for recent or upcoming graduates to succeed in their roles as ECFA members. 

Key events included a workshop on "Publishing Your Research" where participants learned the essentials of scientific writing from experienced authors, and a session on "Project Management for Careers in Funded Research" where panel members shared their perspectives on project leadership and collaboration. These events not only provided valuable knowledge but also created opportunities for early career researchers to connect and exchange ideas within the ECFA community. 

As the panel prepares to collect feedback from its members through a survey, it encourages all eligible individuals to participate and share their thoughts and opinions. This feedback will serve as a basis for developing new activities and initiatives tailored to meet the evolving needs of early career researchers within ECFA.

The unique properties of 2D materials enable spontaneous optical mode confinement, which can be fine-tuned through their structural design in the optical domain. Building upon this concept, our research focuses on developing an innovative optical source with 2D spontaneous four-wave mixing (FWM) functionality. A graphene element drives a non-linear interaction within an hollow silicon nitride waveguide, resulting in the generation of line waves with high coupling efficiency and narrow spectral lines. By optimizing the graphene patch's geometry, its thermal energy can effectively activate carrier interband transitions, thereby enhancing the non-linear behavior of the system. Consequently, a significant FWM coupling factor and minimal loss are achieved, yielding an optical parametric amplifier with exceptional stability and low dispersion properties. This design presents a new pathway for developing robust and integrated optical sources with 2D materials.

The integration of Federated Learning with learning from demonstration allows a single artificial neural network to be trained in a decentralized manner, connecting multiple robots to a shared environment. This setup enables multiple robots and their human operators to collaborate and adapt simultaneously. A demonstrated-based learning framework was implemented for each robot, enabling them to learn and improve their task capabilities. A central server, trained using a large dataset, sends adjustable control parameters to the robots, allowing them to adapt their behavior in response to changing circumstances. A study involving multiple robots and their operators in a navigation task demonstrated the effectiveness of this novel training method on robustness and performance. Compared to traditional training methods, the Federated Learning framework was found to enhance the team's collective ability to adapt to various tasks.

This research introduces a novel estimator for the high-frequency component of a multivariate time series, achieving efficient estimation while addressing the challenge of smoothness in the bias-corrected estimation framework. A stochastic process, specifically the homogeneous Poisson white noise, is utilized as an estimating equation to yield a smooth bias-reduced estimator. The estimator's asymptotic distribution is outlined and its scale and smoothness are analyzed. Simulation experiments validate the theoretical findings and demonstrate the estimator's accuracy when data is sparse. The estimator's utility is illustrated through a real-world analysis of COVID-19 cases in the United States.

Knowledge graph link prediction, which aims to identify unconnected entities with a high probability of being related, has become a critical challenge in knowledge graph completion. Most existing KLP methods focus on either relation extraction or knowledge graph construction, neglecting the interconnectedness of entities. This work presents a new KLP approach called EXERT, which incorporates extracted relations to enhance the prediction of new links. EXERT utilizes a hierarchical model that recognizes the core concepts within knowledge graphs. It achieves this by first detecting primary entities and then assigning corresponding relations. This entailing model is then activated to introduce adaptive variables representing the connections between entities. Finally, a link predictor is trained to identify potential relationships. By merging the entities and relations, EXERT predicts new links with high accuracy. This method was evaluated on two datasets and showed significant improvements over state-of-the-art KLP methods.

The study examines the causal perturbative kernel for zero baryonic chemical potential at Debye mass type $M_p^2 = 2p^2 + (2n+1)\pi i\mu_b$ with $p, n \in \mathbb{Z}_0$. It's observed that introducing baryonic chemical potential reduces the number of Debye mass types to four: $0^2$, $1^2$, $2^2$ and $3^2$. Further analysis focuses on the fermionic kernel at order $\alpha_s^2$ for all four Debye mass types, evaluating its imaginary part to determine collision rates of fermions and antifermions.

The detailed magnetic arrangements within the compounds Tb3RuO7 and Nd3RuO7 have been thoroughly examined through a combination of neutron diffraction, nuclear resonance momentum spectroscopy, and self-consistent electronic structure calculations. In both substances, the Ru ions exhibit antiferromagnetic ordering but with distinct configurations: one where the Ru1 ions are magnetically aligned and the other where they are not, versus the opposite occurring in the other. This unique feature sets the two substances apart from other similar compounds. The driving force behind this magnetic arrangement is likely the distinct orbital states of the Ru ions. The identified orbital moments have confirmed that both substances belong to the P4/mmm symmetry category. The determined parameters will aid in understanding the electronic structure of these compounds in greater detail.

Our investigation into local functionals of data aims to clarify the generalization capabilities of models represented as weighted sums of isolated signal components. We focus on two key factors: 1) the effectiveness of our model in approximating the available training data and 2) the likelihood of our model accurately representing new, unseen data. Under specific conditions, we establish a concentration inequality that measures the first factor and derive a confidence interval for the second factor, demonstrating that our representation achieves nearly perfect generalization when dealing with low-dimensional signals. We further illustrate the improvement in generalization through a theoretical comparison of our local functional representation with a global function representation, with the difference being the way individual data points are combined. Through this comparison, we highlight the potential for improved generalization in models represented locally.

We present a novel, semi-generative approach called CoExGlobe, that uses conformal embedding to model global relationships between multiple variables. This method models each variable as a node in a graph, where adjacent variables and their interactions are represented, and incorporates statistical information about each variable's causes and effects into the modeling process. This causes-effects perspective differs from traditional time-series and dynamic modeling focus on effects and causes. CoExGlobe has been effectively applied in understanding the behavior of complex systems in fields such as biology and social sciences, and has been used to identify key regulators in models of global relationships.

Deep learning's widespread adoption can be attributed to its computational efficiency and adaptability. Despite these successes, the geometric structure underlying deep learning models remains poorly understood. In this study, we delve into the geometric framework underlying deep learning systems, examining the geometry of deep learning models and their training processes. Our in-depth analysis provides a unified perspective on deep learning through geometric modeling, which enables the design of novel algorithms and data structures building on geometric insights. We also explore potential applications of geometric modeling in deep learning, including the development of more effective learning methods.

Consider a cubic field of discriminant $D$ and let $\mathfrak{p}$ be a prime ideal of the ring of integers in this field, with principalization properties. We provide conditions on the radicands $\{a,b,c\}$ that influence the lattice minima within the field, particularly examining how their values relate to the potential critical polynomials associated with $\mathfrak{p}$.

Deep neural networks are inherently difficult to interpret due to their complex internal workings. Despite advancements such as reversible neural networks and interpretive methods like layerwise relevance propagation, a universal solution has yet to be found. We introduce an alternative approach, known as the universal neural network interpreter (UNI), that employs an additional neural network to provide clear insights into its counterpart's decision-making processes. We allow UNI to be trained either before or after a deep neural network's (DNN) training, or concurrently, and demonstrate its versatility by revealing how individual DNN layers contribute to learning by continuously training half of a UNI layer at a time.

The \(r\)-associated Stirling numbers of the second kind, denoted by \(\tilde{S}(m,n;r)\), are a mathematical concept used to define the \(\tilde{F}_r(m,n)\) objects of importance, serving as key components in studying enumerative combinatorics. Several previous studies have focused on investigating \(\tilde{S}(m,n;r)\) with fixed \(r\) or fixed \(r\) and varying \(m\). This research builds upon this foundation by exploring the \(\tilde{S}(m,n;r)\) with fixed \(r\) and varying both \(m\) and \(n\), further enriching the already established results.

Following the development of a theoretical framework for describing phonons within layered materials, researchers applied the framework to a specific case: monolayer graphene. Graphene was found to have a limited number of possible symmetries due to its structure and these symmetries were categorized. Derivatives of graphene, such as chemical variants and bilayers with added atoms, were examined to see how they affect the material's properties. Calculations of electron-phonon interactions revealed that certain modes of vibration could move at speeds similar to those of sound waves, while others could potentially become "relativistic."

We examine the relationship between the uncertainty principle and the properties of a manifold that represents the phase-space for quantum systems. Utilizing the geometric approach proposed by Witte and co-authors, we show that the maximum momentum resolution is directly proportional to the manifold's diameter, with a proportionality constant related to the de-Broglie wavelength. This relationship implies that the product of the minimum spatial and momentum uncertainties is proportional to the square of the manifold's thickness, with the proportionality constant dependent on the curvature. This work generalizes earlier research and provides a unified explanation for the apparent exception.

We suggest utilizing the efficiency of Monte Carlo simulations by employing complex-valued affine coupling layers in generative models. Existing methods have relied on real-valued coupling layers, which have been optimized but computationally costly. Our proposal involves dividing the coupling layer into two components: a pre-sigmoid affine transformation that can be efficiently calculated in bulk using complex arithmetic, and a gating layer, which is applied separately to real and imaginary components. This approach allows for a significant reduction in computational cost, making it feasible to employ widely used Riemannian Monte Carlo methods that were previously hindered by the high expense of evaluating the coupling layer. Our experiments have shown that the proposed system achieves optimal results in generating isotropic log-normal distributions, particularly when using a Riemannian Monte Carlo search method that constrains sample distance.

We present a realistic model featuring a novel geometric arrangement of extra dimensions that incorporates both spatial extension and flavor differentiation. The model employs a U(1)_F flavor symmetry that is broken in a way that produces a significant mass disparity between quarks of different flavors. Primarily, we observe that the radial expansion of the extra dimension influences flavor characteristics. A slightly compressed extra dimension for the top quark and a more expanded geometry for the bottom quark can explain their respective mass ratios. Furthermore, we suggest that the Higgs doublet also resides within the bulk of the extra dimension. Consequently, we find that the bulk radius for the top quark is approximately 7 inverse GeV, whereas the bulk radius for the bottom quark is about 25 inverse GeV. In addition, we find that the bulk arrangement offers a natural explanation for the lightness of the Higgs field, specifically requiring a bulk radius of approximately 4 inverse GeV. Consequently, we expect the electroweak symmetry to be broken at an intermediate radius, roughly in the middle between the bulk and the brane. Consequently, we propose a novel framework for the symmetry breaking of the electroweak interaction, specifically requiring the presence of a geometric feature that splits the extra dimension into two distinct sections. Consequently, we expect the mass hierarchy of the W boson and the top quark to be generated by the difference in their respective mass ratios, specifically requiring a bulk radius of approximately 25 inverse GeV for the

This paper investigates the security implications of maliciously created Virtual PCP Addresses (VPPAs) in cloud-based virtual networks. Although existing work has explored the concept of VPPAs, it primarily focused on their benefits and did not thoroughly examine potential threats. Our research delves into how malicious entities can misuse VPPAs, leading to problems such as resource theft, network congestion, and compromised VM reliability. To address these issues, we propose an enforcement framework that monitors VPPA-related traffic and prevents malicious activity. This framework includes rules to restrict the creation and deletion of VPIs/VPNs, as well as the examination of packets within these malicious VPIs/VPNs. Additionally, we outline a lightweight solution to achieve the required traffic inspection without substantial performance overhead. This proposed enforcement framework serves as a necessary safeguard against the malicious misuse of VPPAs.

The versatility of pre-trained language models is often hampered by their limited
understanding of languages other than English, hindering their widespread use.
To gauge the learnability of language models and their adaptability to unfamiliar
languages, we developed a comprehensive framework that incorporates multiple
variables, including the number of available examples, the model type, its size,
whether it has been fine-tuned, and the degree of similarity between the target
language to English. Using this framework, our study examined the time it takes
for L1 English speakers to adapt pre-trained language models to novel German and
Spanish sentences, exploring how these processes intersect. The research sheds
light on the dynamics of language model adaptability and provides a foundation for
investigating other aspects of language model versatility.

Despite the discrepancy, core collapse supernovae are thought to produce either rotating cores or explosive binaries.  We examine the production of rotating cores in binary systems within a common envelope evolution framework.  Using a detailed numerical simulation, we observe that as a binary system's mass increases, the ratio of its kinetic energy to gravitational energy within the rotating core decreases, indicating that supersonic rotating cores are unlikely.  However, we also note the possibility of a binary system emerging from a common envelope evolution with properties similar to those required for neutron star binaries, including a kinetic energy to gravitational energy ratio around 0.4.  This suggests that such systems could become rotating cores, and further study is warranted to investigate this process in more detail.

The construction of the m-ar-K function offers a novel, efficient method for dimensionality reduction across various applications. Unlike conventional symmetric functions, such as parzen windows or Gaussian mixtures, the m-ar-K function leverages differential entropy to select its parameters, striking a balance between simplicity and effectiveness. Notably, the proposed method requires fewer support vectors than traditional approaches, leading to improved performance in terms of runtime efficiency and generalization capabilities. Building on this foundation, this paper extends the concept of the m-ar-K function to its kernelized form, illustrating its potential application in kernelized mean field approximations for modeling complex data distributions.

A recent proposal for EPC (Extended Polynomial Calculus) defines a family of algebraic decision problems that is more comprehensive than GCSP (General Conjunctive Query Satisfaction Problem). It was claimed that any super-polynomial EPC lower bound implies that PTIME is not contained in CPT (Complement-Time). We demonstrate that a super-polynomial EPC lower bound actually suggests the incompressibility of SAT, leading to major consequences, such as the PNE (P-time Non-Equivalence) conjecture, which would render many algebraic and logical satisfaction problems resistant to efficient solution by Turing machine. Furthermore, we show that even a polynomial EPC lower bound for binary GCSP implies the incompressibility of majorities, a finding we analyze in relation to previous papers by Buss and Zax. Our work introduces a new notion of circuit size for satisfiability problems, referred to as Mon-Maj-circ, and establishes a super-polynomial lower bound for its own problem (Mon-Maj-circ-SAT). We explore Mon-Maj-circ as a potential alternative model of computation that lies between PTIME and CPT, proposing the Mon-Maj (Monotone Majority Circuit) conjecture, which asserts that any CPT algorithm for it would render SAT computable within CPT, thereby resolving the PNE conjecture.

We define a subalgebra class where every member satisfies a particular ideal criterion, thereby including all commutative polynomial algebras over rational numbers. A specific property is shown to be invariant under isomorphic transformations for members of this class, and they are classified based on the presence or absence of a particular type of zero divisor. Moreover, for each of these algebras, we determine the maximum number of ideal components, and in the case where the absence of zero divisors imposes additional structure on these algebras, we find that an equivalence relation applies to their components.

The sheer scale of information shared on social media renders it impossible to comprehend the collective consciousness, thereby hindering informed decision-making. To facilitate more nuanced online discussions, it is crucial to grasp the underlying narratives driving public opinion. By combining natural language processing and network analysis, we uncover the dominant stories shaping social media posts, thereby revealing their functional purpose. Our proposed Graph-based Narrative Extraction Algorithm effectively extracts narratives from vast social media datasets, as demonstrated by a case study analyzing tweets on COVID-19 vaccine acceptance. This study showcases how graph representation learning can distill the complex patterns within social media data, revealing how narratives are linked to specific topics and their respective degrees of popularity.

We introduce a novel event detection system capable of processing spatio-temporal data across multiple dimensions. Existing multi-task deep learning models often overlook the differences in spatial resolutions or ignore temporal correlations. In contrast, our proposed framework combines spatio-temporal convolutional neural networks to identify distinct events with varying spatial scales. Building on this idea, we develop two detection methods: one involves integrating discrete event representations through learned embedding, and the other involves using a sparse matrix to describe event configurations. To demonstrate the efficacy of our approach, we apply it to detecting objects within 3D LiDAR data, specifically focusing on detecting cars and pedestrians. Our model is trained end-to-end using a sparse matrix, allowing it to effectively detect objects regardless of spatial resolution. Experimental results reveal that our proposed framework outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in terms of detection accuracy. Additionally, we perform ablation analysis on event representation and find that combining low-resolution and high-resolution features significantly enhances our proposed method's performance.

This analysis combines the Planck 2015 temperature and lensing data with four datasets, including measurements of galaxy clusters, galaxy distributions, and ISW signals from Planck and WISE, as well as a measurement of the clustering of galaxy distributions from SDSS. This combination allows for a comprehensive examination of six cosmological parameters, including the angular scale of the universe, the amplitude of density fluctuations, the matter density, the amplitude of mass-less neutrinos, the amplitude of mass fluctuations from non-linear regime, and the amplitude of non-linear mass fluctuations. This analysis also investigates potential biases in galaxy distributions for three types of galaxies, as well as examining the impact of residual foregrounds on CMB data. This examination is conducted under two scenarios: one where parameters are treated as completely separate entities, and another where some parameters are allowed to be correlated. This analysis finds that while the addition of CMB lensing data improves the precision of parameter estimates, it also introduces slight biases. This effect is most pronounced in estimates of bias levels for galaxies, as well as estimates of matter density and amplitude of mass-less neutrinos. This analysis further finds that while the agreement between CMB and non-CMB data is generally good, there are some discrepancies, as well as slight preferences for specific parameter ranges, as indicated by the likelihood profiles. Finally, this analysis finds that the examination of residual systematic effects, as well as contamination from Galactic emissions, reveals that these effects have little impact on the estimates of cosmological

Deep neural networks have considerable potential for abuse if their predictions can be manipulated through deliberate deception, a problem that has generated significant research interest. Existing countermeasures, however, primarily focus on enhancing the robustness of models against various types of attacks. Unlike previous approaches, this research develops a new framework for enhancing the robustness of models against the most adverse perturbations. This framework consistently yields models that are more resistant to manipulation while maintaining better performance and improved reliability in the face of uncertainty. Moreover, this research presents a new test to evaluate a model's robustness against the most adverse perturbations by building on the \emph{BREEZE} benchmark. Notably, this test reveals that models optimized using the proposed framework consistently provide more robust predictions even at distances beyond the typical $\pm 8$, and can be up to 14\% more reliable when predicting with uncertainty.

To capture the spread dynamics of rumors, a time-varying diffusion network is constructed by integrating online public opinions and location data. The plant's characteristics such as popularity and longevity are modeled as the output of spatial spatial diffusion, influenced by precursor information and location, and are assumed to follow specific trajectories. The problem of determining the peak and attenuation coefficients of rumors is then formulated as an open-loop optimal control problem, and a pair of stochastic Ricatti equations are derived to determine the optimal trajectory. Unlike existing methods which simply consider the peak and ignore attenuation, or focus on optimal control but overlook the dynamics of precursor information, this work simultaneously determines the peak and attenuation coefficients by taking into account the time-varying network structure and precursor information. The numerical results show that location information significantly affects the peak and attenuation coefficients, and that optimal control can increase the attenuation coefficient while reducing the peak.

Dimensionality reduction techniques play a significant role in enhancing hyperspectral pixel classification efficiency.  Among these methods, different component substitution and component replacement techniques have gained considerable attention.  Notably, methods like PCA, KPCA, ICA, and DL have been found to retain more signal information and offer better neighborhood preservation, which contributes to improved hyperspectral pixel classification.  Building on these findings, this study aims to investigate the potential of DL with its variants, such as DL with CNN, and DL with transfer learning, in dimensionality reduction and hyperspectral pixel classification.  The results show that DL achieves better neighborhood preservation and reduces dimensionality while resulting in more accurate hyperspectral pixel classification when compared to methods like ICA and KPCA.  The application of DL with CNN and transfer learning adds an additional layer of complexity and reduces the dimensionality of the data, leading to neighborhood downgrading in exchange for better model generalization, ultimately resulting in less neighborhood preservation.  The study also demonstrates that DL achieves better results than methods like PCA, ICA, and KPCA, and leads to more accurate hyperspectral pixel classification when compared to methods like LLE, LLNE, and NNE.

Deep neural networks (DNNs) possess exceptional representation capabilities, yet their complex structure renders them difficult to deploy on resource-constrained devices.  To overcome these challenges, researchers have developed several methods to effectively deploy DNNs on edge devices, including efficient model design and compression techniques.  Model compression involves reducing the size of DNNs without sacrificing their performance.  In this category, quantization, pruning, and compacting methods have gained significant attention.  An in-depth review of DNN compression is presented, focusing on recent advancements in single-step compression and zero-cost methods.  Additionally, we analyzed the emerging trends in DNN compression and proposed a new direction for single-step compression, incorporating knowledge distillation.  Our conclusion offers future research directions for DNN compression.

Protein structures determined through experimental methods like X-ray crystallography often contain errors. To improve the accuracy of structures, experts refine them using advanced algorithms. However, these refinements sometimes introduce artificial peptide bond distortions, which can be corrected using high-quality structures as guides. The ProCS (Protein Conformation Sampling) method generates accurate structures of protein regions by leveraging data from high-resolution structures. In a study, researchers combined ProCS with Rosetta structure refinement to create an enhanced method. When tested on refined protein structures, this new method outperformed existing standards, particularly for proteins with distorted peptide bonds. This improved approach reduced errors in structure refinement and performed better than previously developed methods in tests.

In the field of Deep Learning, least squares methods have become widely accepted for training neural networks, particularly due to their robustness in handling noisy targets and data augmentation. However, this popularity may have diverted attention from other relevant loss functions, such as KL Divergence, which, as we demonstrate, can result in superior outcomes. Utilizing simple neural networks trained with an automatic differentiation solver for least squares, we conducted an extensive study to compare various loss functions via a straightforward 'pick-the-best' approach. Our experiments cover 45 comparison scenarios and reveal that, contrary to expectations, more under-represented loss functions, such as KL Divergence and hinge loss, achieve better generalization, despite generally being harder to optimize than least squares. Additionally, we found that on harder datasets, such as those involving more aggressive data transformation or dirty data, KL Divergence results in superior outcomes, as evidenced by both top-performing model accuracy and robustness in model-weight generalization. Conversely, on easier datasets with smooth priors, least squares' reputation for ease of optimization appears to translate to better performance. Interestingly, our study also identifies trends indicating that cross-entropy, commonly used for classification, tends to achieve better results when compared to its hinge loss counterpart, highlighting the challenges associated with overfitting classification targets. Our findings suggest that, although least squares has earned a respected place in the DL toolkit, other loss functions, such as KL Divergence, can deliver superior outcomes in top-per

We examine the basing of the parquet theorem on the Hamiltonian and its implications for amplitude construction. By comparing the Hamiltonian-derived model amplitude with the standard parquet amplitude, we find that the latter lacks certain crucial symmetries, such as conservation and crossing symmetry. The incorporation of higher-loop corrections within the Hamiltonian-derivative model is also investigated. Although it maintains conservation, the resulting amplitude does not fulfill crossing symmetry. Our findings highlight the importance of considering underlying microscopic models for mathematical consistency.

Starting with one monolayer of titanium, we utilize a realistic holographic core Hamiltonian, derived from density functional theory, and investigate the properties of exciton condensation in relation to a pre-existing charge-density-wave state. Our findings demonstrate that exciton condensation occurs under normal-stake lattice conditions and we analyze the impact of lattice vibrations, introducing an effective mass for excitons. For the primary peak in the exciton spectrum, this effective mass significantly deviates from the bare carrier mass, while various many-body corrections lead to a diverse range of possible values. Our study also examines exciton condensation in a pre-thermalized state with an existing density-wave and shows that exciton currents may coexist with density currents under specific circumstances. Our findings suggest that exciton condensation could be realized in 2D transition-metal dichalcogenides with a pre-existing density-wave state.

Emergency dispatch centers around the world rely on advanced computer systems to process and respond to incidents reported via various channels, including texts. To help dispatchers quickly locate critical information about each event, many systems organize incident data into predefined categories and limit editing options for each category. Since users often struggle to predict these categories and format their messages properly, many incidents are misclassified, which can lead to increased editing time. To speed up risk reporting, we designed a system that automatically detects categories and formats text for users, reducing both editing time and incident processing time. Building on existing research, our system utilizes machine learning to analyze reported incidents and their associated metadata. The result is a system that automatically recognizes categories and formats over 80% as accurate in a real-world dataset, with dispatchers only occasionally requiring manual correction.

Following a long-standing theory, a connection between the topological characteristics of a Fermi surface and magnetic properties in superconductors has been established. Specifically, we found that the persistent currents induced by a magnetic field are controlled by the changes in the Fermi surface topology as the field is applied or decreased. As the field causes the Fermi surface to break or merge with other branches, the current undergoes corresponding discontinuous changes, resulting in sharp peaks in the magnetic susceptibility at specific field values. Our findings are reinforced by calculations using a realistic model of the superconductor Pb.

Active learning algorithms allow you to efficiently select a limited number of unlabeled samples to optimize a supervised model's performance within a series of iterations. Minimax entropy-based active learning methods are popular due to their simplicity and effectiveness in choosing optimal samples that maximize diversity and uncertainty. However, these algorithms rely on a global knowledge of the unlabeled data distribution, requiring the re-estimation of this distribution after each iteration, which significantly increases their computational complexity. Additionally, they are usually susceptible to noisy data and can be easily deceived by generating artificial data to manipulate their outcome. In this research, a new semi-supervised minimax entropy-based active learning algorithm is proposed, which uses a modular approach consisting of two separate neural networks to select the most informative unlabeled samples more efficiently while withstanding adversarial attacks. The algorithm minimizes the cross-entropy loss of the estimated and true data distribution without requiring access to the unlabeled data distribution, thus significantly reducing its complexity. The introduced algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art active learning methods on various real-world datasets and is more resistant to attacks compared to existing deep learning-based methods.

The unique sound or character of a voice or instrument is known as timbre. Through technology, it's possible to analyze and mimic this sound. This study measured how similar the timbre is in popular songs using a new approach and found that despite expected variations over the decades, the data showed steady patterns of similarity. Using a different method, the study also studied which instruments were used in which songs from 1950 to 2010 and found that the use of instruments changed gradually over the decades. Based on these results, the study predicted that the time period of a song can be identified with at least 90% accuracy.

We analyze a stochastic bandit process with B arms where, upon occurrence, each arm $i$ receives a reward $R_i$ drawn from a finite set ${\Omega_i}$. The reinforcement process for each arm is independent and memoryless. Our results show that with sufficiently large time horizon $t$, the number of active blocks in the reinforcement sequence for each arm grows almost surely towards the total number of outcomes ${\Omega_i}$ as $t$ approaches infinity, provided that ${\Omega_i}$ is countably infinite and has at least two distinct values, and that the underlying probability distribution over ${\Omega_i}$ is not concentrated at a single value.

Cutting knowledge dates back to December 2022. In proof-theoretic semantics, Cut has a fundamental role as a contained instance of contrapositive preservation (Con), with Con being a more comprehensive principle. This article explores Cut's relationship to preservation of contrapositives. It begins by establishing that Cut follows logically from the contraction lemma, then investigates the converse by analyzing the proof-theoretic implications of contraction within cut-free calculus. Additionally, the article considers how Cut's relationship to Con might be expressed through means of controlled quantification and mediation.

Using human feedback effectively is a critical area of study for accelerating reward learning.  Under an assumption that human feedback is perfect, past research has centered on how to structure comparisons.  This paper, however, investigates the benefits of grouping agents for comparative feedback.  By examining the effects of different comparison groupings, we find that those that split training agents by performance tend to be more efficient than random grouping methods.  This, in turn, suggests that performance-based batching is a viable approach for leveraging human resources and streamlining the reward learning process.

The Smyth powerspace is defined as the category of all subobjects of a given corecompact space, with morphisms established through a monoidal relation. This construction was initially explored by Andrew Smyth in relation to subspaces of compact spaces. The powerspace's compactness properties were later studied by A. Ahmadzai and A. Smyth. Their research revealed that the Smyth powerspace of a core-compact space is an exponentiable functor, facilitating the construction of a monoidal closed category. While this construction maintains core-compactness properties for certain spaces, it does not universally do so. In fact, it was demonstrated that the Smyth powerspace of a core-compact extremally discrete space does not yield an extremally discrete space. However, we found that the Smyth powerspace of an extremally discrete space does yield a weakly algebraicbic monoidal category. By defining a suitable topology on the set of all subobjects of an extremally discrete space, we can ensure that the Smyth powerspace falls within a specific category, maintaining its core-compact properties in the process.

The behavior of vortex loops in a two-dimensional ideal flow is examined with loops capable of rotating and carrying a finite Dirac mass distribution on their surface, representing a fraction of the enclosed area. A modified configuration space is introduced, consisting of oriented loops with variables including the area they encompass, their orientation, and the distribution of their Dirac mass. A detailed analysis of this space's structure, particularly its geometric properties, is given, along with a comprehensive calculation of its Dirac currents. These currents are shown to represent the loop's self-linking number and its interaction with a fixed point, providing a precise mathematical formulation. As a result, the analysis offers a novel method for detecting loops that encompass a predetermined area and have a specified self-linking number. Additionally, it yields an algorithm for counting the number of loops meeting specified conditions.

Omission of regularization in learning representations can lead to subpar performance in downstream tasks. In time-series analysis, a specific AIPW estimator is commonly impaired by high dimensional issues, yet little attention has been given to developing a regularized variant. This research introduces a first-of-its-kind AIPW estimator, subject to group lasso and its extensions, applicable to time-series data with at least two dimensions. Theoretical proofs confirm the consistency and asymptotic normality of this novel estimator. Empirical evaluations on artificial and real-world data demonstrate the AIPW estimator's robustness and adaptability across various models, datasets, and regularization settings. Additionally, the results highlight the estimator's capacity to mitigate overfitting and improve AIPW estimator's fundamental limitations.

The vector tau particle, consisting of three flavors of quarks, serves as an ideal candidate for lattice study due to its larger mass in comparison to the pi and rho particles. A new, two-step Monte Carlo simulation method for tau decay processes involves generating meson pairs and then selecting those that decay into a tau particle. To enhance computational efficiency, this study focuses on a technique for directly generating tau particle spectra without the need for two separate Monte Carlo simulations. Two different tricks are presented to directly generate tau particle spectra, including one approach based on a known rho-pi correlation and the other using a response function to the tau particle. Results from lattice QCD using the lattice vector gauge field, obtained by the lattice QCD project with 2+1 dynamical quark flavors, serve as input for these studies. Applications of these tricks facilitate direct tau particle spectrum generation, and the resulting spectra show promising consistency with current experimental findings.

Our study focuses on understanding how baroclinic waves develop and behave within a rotating annulus with a vertically varying temperature pattern, and we analyze their surface expression, such as circulation patterns, temperature differences, and geostrophic flow directions. To investigate these dynamics, we employed a diagnostic analysis, considering both analytical and numerical approaches, as described in a companion paper, and we emphasize the importance of examining wave dynamics at different vertical intervals, especially between the surface and the mid-levels, as well as the analysis of the boundary layers at the inner and outer walls.

This study proposes a Bayesian method for estimating extreme value models, specifically the Generalized Pareto Distribution, based on homogeneity assumptions. A parameter in the models is tuned using Tikhonov regularization, influencing both model estimation and likelihood calculations. A novel Markov Chain Monte Carlo sampling method is developed for obtaining posterior distributions. Notably, the tuning parameter is critical and must be carefully selected; this study explores optimal choices using cross-validation and a Bayesian approach. The method is tested with simulated data and applied to wind speed anomalies from the UK's Cramer meteorological station.

We approach corruption robust reinforcement learning by assuming that the model contains hidden corruption. To survive in this environment, we develop an algorithm that adapts the corrupted model's reward parameter without knowing the degree or extent of corruption. Although epsilon, the measure of corruption, is unknown, we establish an algorithm that is robust to a certain amount of corruption, epsilon. This adapted algorithm is resilient to corruption amount up to epsilon, but its performance may decline as epsilon approaches zero. Our method involves learning a set of potential models rather than a single model. By using a bound on the Leamning period, we ensure that the algorithm's performance does not diminish as epsilon approaches zero. Our method also incurs an exponential increase in computational efficiency. Our method's efficiency and performance are analyzed under the assumption that corruption follows uniform distribution. Under this assumption, we show that our method is robust to up to epsilon = 1/27 and demonstrate that its performance may decline as epsilon approaches zero. Our method's efficiency and performance are analyzed under the assumption that corruption follows uniform distribution. Under this assumption, we show that our method is robust to up to epsilon = 1/27 and demonstrate that its performance may decline as epsilon approaches zero.

The impulsive heat equation is a model that incorporates sudden changes into the standard heat equation. It has real-world applications in physics, biology, and economics. Our study investigates the impulse approximate controllability of this equation, which involves using impulsive controls to approximate exact controllability. Specifically, we established an error estimate for impulse approximate controllability and demonstrated that small impulsive energies enable precise controllability. Moreover, our analysis highlights the distinct role of impulse controls in approximating steep fronts within the equation's parameters.

Detecting predictions made outside the training distribution is crucial for ensuring a system's reliability. Techniques for identifying such predictions rely heavily on measuring the consistency of a model's predictions, often using metrics like maximum likelihood or Bayesian methods. However, these methods fall short in detecting anomalies, particularly where data is generated through targeted transformations. A new method, OODivorce, has been developed, which operates by training a set of auxiliary models to generate data in the presence of a given input - these auxiliary models can introduce a range of minor distortions. When the main model fails to recognize its generated counterparts as part of its original distribution, it indicates that the input lies outside that distribution. OODivorce has demonstrated exceptional performance on a range of benchmark datasets and, importantly, has been proven to generalize effectively. Furthermore, empirical evidence confirms that learning from generated data in conjunction with real data enables the model to distinguish between in-distribution and out-of-distribution data with ease, even without receiving explicit labeling. In fact, training on generated data alone proves sufficient for accurately identifying anomalies, provided the generator has been trained on a range of target transformations. As such, OODivorce offers a robust and effective solution for detecting anomalies, accompanied by a new benchmark dataset featuring data generated via multiple transformations.

Universality of molecular motor dynamics has been observed across different systems. This phenomenon is investigated by analyzing the motion of an asymmetric top driven by rotational Brownian motion and an asymmetrical potential. The results show that forced molecular motor dynamics can be reduced to a specific dimensionless equation, applicable to all motor types, regardless of their geometric or electrical characteristics. This universal description facilitates the prediction of exotic motion patterns and links together seemingly distinct systems.

A one-way word transducer with a bounded, regular resynchronizer is introduced, allowing any non-deterministic two-way word transducer to be converted into an equivalent variant. This type of resynchronizer acts as an origin indicator during processing and includes a bounded sequence of origin markers that can be overwritten and preserved. It operates within a confined space at the start of the string and has a limited capacity that can be expanded linearly with an accompanying modification. It is further demonstrated that a specific type of bounded resynchronizer, which includes two origin markers, is insufficient for equivalent transformations.
Our analysis reveals that calculating a specific entry in the f-Convolving matrix can be done in $O(n)$ time, significantly more efficiently than computing the entire convolving matrix.

Our atmospheric analysis of GJ 229B, a benchmark object of its kind, provides crucial insights into its formation and help clarify the planetary-star boundary. Our findings are based on an atmospheric model that accounts for variability in cloud cover, featuring two atmospheric layers with distinct radial temperature gradients. This model was tested across different parameters in various scenarios, with the results indicating that atmospheres devoid of super-Jovian properties are unlikely. A surrounding disk or close-in stellar companion is thought to be necessary for powering GJ 229B's internal gravitational energy. Our study focuses on comparing GJ 229B's characteristics to those of recently discovered T/dwarf samples, highlighting its distinct features. Two key potential targets for upcoming direct imaging missions like the James Webb Space Telescope are suggested as promising candidates for a thorough spectral analysis of GJ 229B's atmosphere.

Quark model potentials are tested based on binding energy spectra. This test is conducted using lattice-generated correlation functions and quark model parameters are analyzed and compared to existing studies. The research also examines the potential existence of tetraquark states within a specific region and identifies crucial factors that determine this possibility.

Recent findings in the $C\!P$-violating phase $\phi_{s}$ and $\Delta\phi_{s}$ have been presented at the 2019 Flavor Convention. The value of $\phi_{s}$ as determined from the LHCb's $B^0_s\to J/\psi\bar{B}^0_s$ decay is in agreement with the Standard Model's prediction. This agreement provides the potential to discover new physics up to a scale of 2-3 TeV by limiting new physics' effects on $\phi_{s}$ to less than $10^{-3}$. The LHCb's search for $\Delta\phi_{s}$ in $B^0_s\to J/\psi\bar{B}^0_s$ using off-shell data is also discussed.

To assess the risk of breathing in aerosols, it's crucial to calculate the likelihood of encountering them. Our computation method accurately determines aerosol dispersion by modeling particle trajectories within a 3D space using the fluid dynamics equations. The well-mixed model serves as a straightforward baseline for comparison with more intricate simulations. When comparing the two methods in the context of an infected person, the well-mixed model provides reasonably accurate predictions for average aerosol concentrations and exposure risks. Specifically, for an indoor setting with proper ventilation, the well-mixed model's estimates coincide closely with those from complex simulations. However, for an indoor setting with minimal airflow, the well-mixed model's estimates diverge from those of the complex simulations. Their discrepancy grows with decreasing ventilation rates, corresponding to an increased danger level. Consequently, for an indoor setting with minimal airflow and high respiratory rates, replacing the well-mixed model with a complex simulation could diminish the estimated average exposure by as much as 60%. Our study demonstrates the value of integrating aerosol dynamics into infection risk assessments through a straightforward scenario.

The aim of this study is to gain insight into the nuclear structure of even-even Te isotopes by matching theoretical and experimental $\beta$-decay transition strengths. A theoretical description employing the proton-neutron quasiparticle phonon model is used, with the underlying nuclear structure being modeled with the deformed shell-model based on the Woodside interaction. This approach allows for a thorough comparison between theoretical and experimental data from steady-state $\beta$-decay experiments. The results reveal that steady-state methods can access a range of decay energies, spanning from 0 to 5 MeV, with particular emphasis on identifying collective $\beta$-Vibron transitions. A notable example involves comparing the collective structure of the isotopes $^{137}$Te and $^{135}$Te. The findings from this study support the idea that steady-state $\beta$-decay can serve as a sensitive tool for investigating the nuclear structure of unstable isotopes.

Recently, a set of global attributes has been expanded to include time information, resulting in the creation of new families of exchange programs, including temporal attribute exchange and time-invariant attribute exchange. To further develop uniqueness theorems for these new families, a detection method for exchange program violations was also introduced. This new detection method is based on the 'twin property'. To establish the twin property, two crucial concepts, 'homomorphisms' and 'embeddings', have been defined. The uniqueness theorem for time-invariant attribute exchange programs states that an exchange program violation can be detected automatically by checking if it has a homomorphism onto another instance with the same attributes. The uniqueness theorem for temporal attribute exchange programs requires one more step: it is necessary to verify the presence of an embedding onto another instance with the same attributes. The presence of both homomorphisms and embeddings for a specific detection pattern is also confirmed. Establishing the uniqueness theorems for these new families of exchange programs results in a significant expansion of the potential detection methods for violations, indicating that previously undetected violations may actually be detectable.

The light-light or light-heavy quarkonium systems can be modeled using the potential matrix method, which allows for the calculation of Regge trajectories. In this research, we extend the method to heavy-heavy quarkonium systems. Our analysis reveals that the mass squared of the heavy-heavy quarkonium state, as a function of the principal quantum number, adheres to the Regge trajectory prediction, both for spin-orbit coupling and its absence. Furthermore, our outcomes are in line with conventional Regge theory, according to which the spin is not coupled to the orbital momentum. Additionally, we have derived potential matrices for the heavy-heavy quarkonium systems, which are similar to their light-heavy counterparts. In heavy-heavy quarkonium systems, just like light-heavy ones, the spin-orbit coupling influences the ground state, but does not affect higher states, as their properties are determined solely by orbital movements.

We examine whether Szabados's conjecture holds for the minimal periodic decomposition of patterns with specific properties. Our findings validate the conjecture for patterns that have a complex structure, but not for those with a simple structure. In particular, we provide a counterexample that demonstrates the conjecture does not hold for patterns with a simple structure that has a limited number of periodic components.

A data-driven model reduction technique known as Dynamic Mode Decomposition (DMD) has effectively identified the spatiotemporal patterns underlying nonlinear systems. Despite its efficacy, DMD is limited in its ability to capture the complex behaviors exhibited by nonlinear systems, particularly when the system is fully understood. A Dynamic Mode Decomposition kernel (DMDk) method was introduced to enhance DMD by utilizing the learned patterns from a kernel operator. Although DMDk can capture the nonlinear dynamics, the kernel operator is currently assumed to be a universal approximation network (UAN) with a fixed universal approximation capability. In this research, we present a new kernel operator based on normalizing flows that can refine the nonlinear patterns, and we demonstrate that this new kernel can replicate a wide range of benchmark patterns. Furthermore, we show that combining the patterns with the snapshots can lead to better outcomes when the full system is known, and we propose an iterative process for extracting the system's governing equations. To verify the efficacy of this new kernel, we apply it to two complex systems: a low-energy atmospheric simulation and a high-energy experimental experiment. The results from these experiments demonstrate that the new DMDk method outperforms the traditional DMDk in both cases.

The evaluation of chess openings and player talent has long been a topic of discussion among experts. To quantify this, our research employs the Economic Fitness and Complexity algorithm on a comprehensive chess database, analyzing the strategic moves players make within specific opening frameworks. This approach weighs the effectiveness of individual moves and their combinations, taking into account their historical outcomes to assess their fitness. By combining traditional human judgment with modern data science, we seek to shed new light on the intricacies of chess and its players.

Binary systems consisting of compact objects such as neutron stars or white dwarfs go through a phenomenon known as accretion-induced collapse (AIC), which results in the birth of a new compact star. There are two types of AICs: those involving the growth of a stable compact object that eventually dies as a compact star, and those that lead to the spontaneous collapse of an existing compact object without prior stable growth. The second type of AIC is thought to be the origin of Type Ia supernovae through the collapse of a white dwarf. A possible way for this process to occur is through the symmetric collapse of a massive white dwarf surrounded by an accretion disk. Recent research has shown that such a massive white dwarf can exist if it has a strong magnetic field. In our study, we simulated both the stable growth of a massive white dwarf and its spontaneous collapse. A massive white dwarf with a radius of around 1,000 km and an mass of around 2.0 solar masses is stable, but as its mass increases, it becomes unstable against further growth and eventually collapses under a certain amount of additional accretion. This amount of accretion is found to be around 0.15 solar masses for a 2.0 solar mass massive white dwarf. However, as its mass increases towards the point of chirp point where it becomes a black hole, its accretion efficiency also changes and may lead to instability. Initially, a general method for obtaining first integrals in higher-order Euler-Lagrange ODEs has been established. Subsequently, this method was applied to the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator to derive a first integral, and it was demonstrated that the described approach leads to the known result for this system. Nonetheless, our method appears to be less effective when attempting to find a first integral for the Pais-Uhlenbeck oscillator using different variables. Although we were able to obtain a first integral using our established approach, the calculated result seems to be a previously unidentified expression.

Reaching optimal performance in retrieving 3D shapes from sketches is complicated by the varied appearance of sketches and the need to account for their abstract nature. Unlike image-based models, domain-specific sketch-shape datasets are limited, hindering training and generalization of sketch-specific models. In contrast, pre-trained vision-language models exhibit excellent zero-shot performance in retrieving 3D shapes from sketches, particularly model T2D2. However, applying these models to novel domains requires extensive sketch collection and pairing with the target shapes, an impractical task due to the cost involved. To overcome this shortcoming, we propose T2D2-SE, a two-part approach incorporating T2D2 with pre-trained capabilities and a novel semantic enhancement layer capable of generalizing to novel domains without the need for additional training. In experiments, T2D2-SE surpasses other approaches, including T2D2 and domain-specific models, by a significant margin, with its code and models available for evaluation.

The planet HD80606b, a gas giant, orbits its star every 111 days.  On March 4, 2017, NASA's Spitzer, Hubble, and Keck observatories conducted a coordinated study of this planet as it passed directly in front of its star.  This event was the ninth such occurrence captured by these observatories.  As the planet HD80606b orbits its star, it experiences a dramatic change in temperature - decreasing from 1,700 to 320 kilometers per hour.  During the occultation event observed on March 4, 2017, the Spitzer telescope detected the planet HD80606b's infrared radiation at wavelengths of 4.3 micrometers, revealing its rapid cooling from 1,700 to 1700K.  This occurred as the planet HD80606b accelerated from 32 to 230 kilometers per hour and its atmosphere contracted.  The spectra from the Keck telescope at a wavelength of 4.2 micrometers showed a strong water signature with no signs of a carbon-dioxide presence.  This discovery supports models that suggest carbon dioxide evaporates off the planet as it orbits near its star.  The Keck and Hubble telescopes also detected carbon monoxide and methane in the planet's atmosphere, with no signs of a hydrogen-helium mixture that had been predicted. Observations suggest that rotating supermassive black holes exist at the centers of most galaxies, including our own. The existence of singularities within the interior of a supermassive, rotating black hole is well established. Research has shown that small changes to its mass profile can make the singularity invisible due to a "fuzz ball" effect, where the singularity is obscured by a region known as the event horizon. Consequently, a supermassive black hole's properties are determined by its event horizon rather than its singularity. Building on this work, this study examines whether similar phenomena occur in a collapsing, rapidly rotating fluid. The results indicate that a small perturbation to the fluid's mass profile can make the singularity visible, where it is not protected by an event horizon. Conversely, a small perturbation to a fluid that forms a singular, rotating black hole can make the event horizon visible, where it is not protected by the singularity.

The weak gravity conjecture suggests that the entropy of an extremal black hole should decrease after adding a small amount of charge. This theory is being investigated further by considering a thermodynamic process in which the mass of the black hole decreases in a canonical ensemble. However, our calculations indicate that in a canonical ensemble, the mass of the black hole cannot decrease if it possesses a non-zero magnetic field. Consequently, the weak gravity conjecture does not hold for charged black holes in a canonical ensemble under the influence of an external magnetic field. On the other hand, for unrestrained systems in a grand canonical ensemble, the weak gravity conjecture can be satisfied, provided that the process begins at the ground state and involves the addition of a specified amount of charge relative to the magnetic field. These assumptions are essential for the success of the weak gravity conjecture.

We've developed a novel intrinsic motivation system for reinforcement learning that utilizes the autocorrelation of agent observations to identify consistent patterns in environment dynamics. This discovery-based approach doesn't require any prior knowledge about the system. It also integrates with traditional reward-based training methods, resulting in a more efficient and robust learning process. Our research demonstrates the efficacy of this intrinsic motivation system when combined with reward-based training, leading to a substantial reduction in the number of training steps required to solve complex tasks. Notably, the integration of both intrinsic and extrinsic rewards leads to a significant improvement in training efficiency, particularly when compared to systems relying solely on intrinsic motivation. All the necessary code and demonstration materials are available on our GitHub repository: https://github.com/jaymesmith/IntrinsicMotivation.

In Colored Poincaré gravity, we have developed a fundamental classical particle model, incorporating both massive and massless entities. We have detailed the underlying non-Commutative space, characterizing the inertial mass of these particles through the geometric structure of the model. We have further developed quantum distributions for the particles, incorporating Symbolic methods to derive both conventional and Unconventional Kennedy-type Dirac equations. These models have significant implications for the development of micro-catalysts in Colored gravity, with potential applications in particle physics and cosmology.

We examine the parameterized complexity of finding exact or natural bounds for the longest directed acyclic path in a weighted directed graph. Similar to the $k$-Longest Paths problem on unweighted graphs, it can be solved in $O(c^t \cdot t)$ time, where $t$ is the treewidth plus one. Furthermore, we discover that even on weighted graphs, finding exact or natural bounds for the longest directed acyclic path is a solvable parameterized problem, with $O(c^t \cdot t^2)$ time complexity, by proposing a parameter-fidelity algorithm.
