Improving convergence in optimization algorithms is a long-standing goal in optimization research.  Identifying specific structural properties within the optimization problem, such as differentiability manifolds, provides valuable insight and can accelerate convergence by exploiting this structure.  This work develops a method to identify differentiability manifolds through automatic differentiation of the gradient acquisition process.  A theoretical framework justifying this approach is established.  Furthermore, this technique is demonstrated to enhance the performance of several standard optimization algorithms by approximately aligning them with the identified differentiability manifolds.  Experimental validation across various test functions confirms that this method promotes convergence in almost all cases, even when the structure itself is not exactly known.  Consequently, this technique holds potential as a new strategy for structurally enhanced optimization convergence.

Consider a commutative ring $R$ and prime ideals in $R$ that have properties related to absorption. We characterize weakly $1$-absorbing prime ideals in $R$, demonstrating that the cube of a non-$1$-absorbing prime ideal that is weakly $1$-absorbing is not itself $1$-absorbing unless it is a maximal ideal. We prove that in a weakly $1$-absorbing prime ring with zero product, every non-zero square-free element is contained in a suitable double ideal. We establish that every element in a ring that has properties related to semiprime has a specific minimal prime ideal contained in its annihilator. We show that the intersection of all prime ideals with the property of being weakly $1$-absorbing in a commutative ring $R$ is equal to the annihilator of the set of non-$1$-absorbing prime ideals in $R$.

A point-to-point comparison between experimental and simulated differential photon spectra in various $K^0_S$ momentum bins is conducted, along with the presentation of the factors needed to correct these spectra. This study focuses on events featuring one or more photons and is based on an $e^+e^-$ collision data set, recorded by LHCb using the collision data at center-of-mass energies of 7 and 8 TeV, totaling 3 $10^{12}$ recorded events. The data are then used to investigate the semileptonic decays $K^0_S \to \mu^+ \mu^-$ and $\pi^0 \to \mu^+ \mu^-$, applying a corrected integral to determine the ratio of experimental to simulated cross-sections, with the latter including contributions from muon pairs produced by both hadronic and muon pair production processes. The influence of muon pairs produced via the hadronic process is found to significantly exceed that of the muon pair process in these events. This study identifies hadronic contributions as the primary source of systematic uncertainty in the measurement of the $K^0_S$ and $\pi^0$ mesons' semileptonic decays.

The proposed experiment, known as the Gravitational Radiation Observatory (GRO), aims to detect gravitational waves by measuring the impact of their presence on the diffusion process of neutrons through the use of up-conversion and a neutron time-of-flight technique. The observatory's main diffusion volume will serve as a highly sensitive instrument to detect correlations induced by these waves, allowing for the determination of their direction and potentially shedding new light on astrophysical phenomena, with the advantage of having a shorter expectation time than other detectors. A simulation was carried out to demonstrate the observatory's capability, which showed that it would be able to detect 90% of signals with a minimum signal-to-noise ratio of 2 within a specific frequency range and direction. The study also found that the time it takes for these correlations to be measured will initially be estimated based on a rough prediction and then refined as more data becomes available, with the expectation that more accurate results will be achieved sooner than anticipated with the current estimated time being a conservative one.

In pharmacology, relational machine learning models are being increasingly used, and their power to identify relationships between complex entities in pharmacogenomics is particularly notable. However, assessing the capabilities of these models is a daunting task due to the constraints of predictive confidence ratings. Currently, model performance is primarily evaluated through end-task prediction accuracy on test data, without considering how well they represent relationships in the training data. As a result, there is no guarantee that models with high predictive accuracy necessarily capture the essential relationships for their tasks. To address this, we have introduced a ground-breaking framework that evaluates relational machine learning models based on their ability to accurately represent relationships in training data and apply learned knowledge to unseen test data. Our unique relationship evaluation framework utilizes relational properties and graph embeddings to transform pharmacogenomic datasets into network representations. This enables the comparison of models' predicted relationships with actual knowledge through a comparison of their proximity metrics. To further mimic human intuitive understanding, we also incorporated metrics that measure the models' ability to identify knowledge hierarchies and distribute knowledge points across relevant dimensions. Our framework was successfully applied to four kgp end-task models, where we discovered that models with strong relational capabilities outperformed those with solely predictive skills.

Effective and widespread road condition monitoring systems pose a significant challenge, particularly in developing countries with limited infrastructure. Traditional methods involving in-person assessments are labor-intensive and expensive, while automated solutions often require specialized equipment. This research aims to improve road condition monitoring through a smartphone-based approach, leveraging devices with which most individuals are already familiar. We developed an open-source application that collects relevant data by having drivers slowly traverse along a road, slowing down when they encounter rough terrain. Anomaly detection is then performed on collected images using a pre-trained ResNet model, with an accompanying technical guide available online. Initial results from multiple tests in Colombia indicate that our method achieves acceptable levels of precision and recall, with potential for further improvement through the use of more advanced mobile device capabilities, such as those incorporating better cameras.

Existing solutions to imitation learning assume that agent and expert behaviors can be perfectly mapped from within their respective perspectives.  In reality, domain knowledge is often limited, leading to environments that poorly resemble each other, especially in fields like medical imaging.  Even with the application of visual distortion correction techniques, discrepancies persist, potentially misleading imitation learning agents.  These discrepancies not only hinder the learning process, but they also cause the agent to focus on irrelevant characteristics, rather than discovering the expert's underlying decision logic.  To overcome these challenges, we propose a new approach that learns a joint action-state space by incorporating both an expert action prediction model and a novel state-action discrepancy metric.  By using the learned state-action discrepancy to align the agent's perspective with the expert's, we can bypass the limitations imposed by the domain expert's imperfect environment.  We demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed framework through successful imitation learning on a synthetic POMDP horizon of 20, in comparison to a baseline that struggled with the discrepancy.  Furthermore, we apply our framework to an actual ultrasound-based laparoscopic tool guidance scenario, where we outperform a competitor model that failed to mitigate the discrepancy between the agent and expert environments.

We utilize three-dimensional hydrodynamic simulations to investigate how protostar formation and system angular momentum influence each other in collapsing gas clouds. For this research, we defined a newly formed protostar as a object surrounded solely by an optically thin, thermal boundary layer. Our study reveals that higher angular momentum clouds have a greater chance of disrupting into multiple protostars, especially those with lofted magnetic fields. However, without magnetic influences, clouds with high angular momentum tend to fragment into disks rather than protostars. Notably, we find that around 30% of clouds with bound protostars experience disk fragmentation, highlighting the importance of efficient angular momentum transfer. Efficient transfer also allows for the formation of protostars at smaller radii and lower masses. Efficient angular momentum transfer also results in more symmetrical and conservative mass loss, which in turn enables the protostar to form earlier and with smaller deviations from theoretical predictions.

This research builds on previous findings regarding the redundancy of association rules, particularly those concerning implications among items. This paper expands on that concept, focusing on the entailment relationship among association rules in general. By treating association rules as predicates, we examined the entailment relationship among them and identified its equivalence with the disentailment relationship in terms of contrapositive statements. Additionally, we devised a method for characterizing redundancy among association rules using predicate logic and applied it to simplify rules containing redundant items. Furthermore, we analyzed the computational complexities associated with this approach and demonstrated the efficacy of this method through relevant data sets.

Individuals struggling with mental health issues are overrepresented in the criminal justice system, yet receiving mental health treatment in prison can lower the likelihood of committing the same crime upon release. By leveraging a unique dataset combining crime statistics and mental health patient records, our research achieves record-breaking performance on the task of predicting the effectiveness of mental health treatment for specific crimes. The findings reveal that certain crimes are more responsive to treatment than others, with violent offenses showing a greater decrease in recidivism when treated individuals go on to commit fewer violent crimes upon release. Notably, unsupervised methods were found to provide comparable insight to traditional machine learning approaches, offering an open-source framework that can aid in developing more effective mental health interventions.

This paper uses complex analysis to derive the eight-step closure of a combinatorial identity related to the Laguerre polynomials, specifically the Laguerre polynomial's generating function. By translating the identity into a domain using a biholomorphic mapping, our method allows for a straightforward confirmation of the combinatorial interpretation's correctness.

Creating accurate maps of wireless signal strength across various locations is essential for numerous wireless localization techniques. We introduce a measure for assessing the uncertainty of map measurements that identifies which locations require more data to refine the map. This metric is utilized in an iterative process of collecting and refining map measurements, along with other optimizations. Experimental results show significant improvements in map accuracy when compared to conventional methods such as exploring all locations uniformly. The need for fewer measurements in each iteration allows us to collect and process a smaller dataset, thereby reducing both the computational cost and the time required to generate an accurate map.

One of the major challenges in using anomaly detection methods is the absence of annotated data, making model training difficult.  Despite this obstacle, these methods are critical for identifying unusual patterns in large datasets, such as system failures or network threats. One potential solution to this problem is unsupervised learning, particularly methods utilizing neighbor-based approaches. However, these methods are susceptible to adjustments and hard to interpret. We introduce a novel anisotropic Gaussian-based unsupervised anomaly detection method that addresses data heterogeneity by modeling nearby points as clusters, using local density estimates and theis isotropy. Our method features a straightforward and efficient implementation, despite its computational complexity. We evaluate our method through several experiments on public datasets, where it has shown better performance than established anomaly detection methods.

The current state-of-the-art automatic speech recognition system's performance in verifying provided audio data is significantly impacted by its accuracy in identifying the correct audio source. A recent study evaluated the effectiveness of verification methods in detecting artificially altered audio data and discovered that such alterations often went undetected in high-quality audio even when examined in detail. In response to the need for improved protection, this research compares the capabilities of multiple advanced verification systems in distinguishing original audio files from artificially altered files. The evaluation, which analyzed over 35,000 voice messages related to COVID-19, revealed that a particular system was 74% accurate in identifying unaltered voice messages when the provided audio quality was very high. Notably, this research found that verification systems struggled to consistently recognize altered voice messages when the provided audio quality was low, with accuracy rates varying significantly between systems. The largest discrepancy in performance was over 20%, indicating the value of developing methods that can effectively mitigate extremely low-quality audio.

This study investigates the efficacy of data augmentation methods in natural language processing for smaller training datasets. A straightforward method is employed to enhance a dataset, consisting of altering input tokens, similar to how words are replaced in a word dictionary. This approach is utilized to enhance various NLP benchmarks, showcasing notable enhancements for smaller datasets and no negative impact on larger datasets. Additionally, the method is comparable to more sophisticated data augmentation techniques, resulting in comparable outcomes. Our experiments reveal that this basic approach is highly effective, especially when dealing with limited training data.

This research investigates how a measure of weak convergence, specifically the distance between functions of estimated parameters and their true counterparts, can be computed numerically. We consider statistical models defined by constrained nonlinear equations but focus on an important subset, the exponential families with constraints. To establish the weak convergence distance, we first derive an analysis of the complex parameter space, then apply this to the complex projective space, then utilize these results to calculate the distance, and finally provide a straightforward method for computing it numerically. We then provide several numerical examples to demonstrate the efficiency and accuracy of this method.

The increasing accessibility of Public Data Archives (PDAs) has created opportunities for various applications by enabling global sharing of anonymized data. While encryption methods can ensure the security of individual records, they fail to account for the interdependencies between records, which become apparent when data is processed. As a result, the anonymity of records can be compromised when queried or involved in join operations, potentially leading to significant privacy breaches. This paper introduces the concept of record relationships and establishes a formal framework for evaluating file systems' anonymity. It then proposes the first fully formalized analysis of existing anonymity metrics, revealing inconsistencies and misunderstandings. Based on this analysis, the paper creates a method for determining the minimum amount of noise needed to protect dependent data. Finally, the paper demonstrates that applying noise to interdependent data may require more noise than expected, leading to reduced anonymity. This can be particularly problematic when dealing with high degrees of dependency, as seen in hierarchical or tree-structured data.

Our study utilizes data from the ALMA observatory to analyze the chemical composition in protoplanetary disks. Specifically, we examined C$_2$H in a subset of disks with existing CO emissions maps. By leveraging the C$_2$H/\CO emission ratio, we determined the C/O elemental abundance in these disks, revealing that it ranges from 0.5 to 3.0 times the solar value. However, in the inner disk regions close to the star, this ratio is significantly higher, up to 20 times the solar value. A model incorporating gas-phase metal reactions accurately describes our observations, producing C$_2$H emissions in regions lacking hydrogen-bearing molecules. It also predicts that in the outer disk areas, C$_2$ H can arise from the endogenous gas, a byproduct of the UV photodissociation of CO. We discovered that the C/O elemental abundance in the gas is lower than in solid particles in the disks. As a result, the sublimation temperature of C and O and the point of C$_2$H emission conversion from gas to solids occur at larger radii compared to typical values seen in solid C$_2$H.

Generating large amounts of time-stamped data is becoming increasingly common in scientific research, typically resulting in files exceeding gigabytes in size. Current methods involve visualizing such data in tools like Microsoft Excel or graphical analysis software, yet these often become impractical with large file sizes. In this paper, we introduce the Extensible Time-tag Analyzer (ETA), a web-based platform that processes time-stamped data efficiently, regardless of file size. ETA's compact design allows for rapid development and deployment, while its open-source architecture facilitates customization for specific applications. By employing a straightforward data pipeline, ETA outperforms other solutions in both speed and functionality, making it an ideal choice for time-stamped data analysis. ETA's versatility is demonstrated through two real-world examples, including analyzing time-stamped images from, (1) a MicroManager microscopes, and (2) astrophysical data from the Hubble Space Telescope. ETA's capabilities are available through a public website, where users can upload their data for analysis, view results, and download explanations in various formats.

Mean field games offer an innovative approach to analyzing large-scale systems by leveraging the concept of average behavior to derive equilibrium strategies. However, implementing this idea within a continuous framework presents difficulties due to non-existence of equilibrium in settings that demand continuous solutions. Our research builds upon McKean's original idea and adapts a novel transformation of state and cost functions to address existence concerns. Utilizing a continuous system of ordinary differential equations, we overcome the non-existence issue and establish the existence of an equilibrium, while exploring the impact of irregular cost functions on mean field game theory.

Our research involves an in-depth analysis of the open cluster NGC 663, consisting of multiple stellar strings spanning up to 10 degrees on the sky. We've performed a detailed UV to near-IR photometric study of these stars, leveraging data from Gaia, ASTRI, and various other telescopes. By applying the BSTF analysis method, we determine the cluster's parameters, including distances, luminosities, and masses for 663 stars. The analysis reveals that the cluster members exhibit minimal chemical discrepancies, being chemically homogeneous. The findings also indicate that the cluster strings possess similar properties to nearby field stars. The study of NGC 663's stellar strings shows them to be dynamically older than previously thought, with evidence of dissolved clusters still retaining their spatial structure. Our research supports the idea that stellar strings are a transient stage in cluster evolution, forming through the dynamic friction of multiple clusters in close proximity.

As online social platforms gain popularity, users are increasingly expressing themselves through their appearance, yet detecting inconsistencies in their outfits has remained largely unresolved. To address this, we propose an end-to-end system using a Siamese network to compare fashion outfit images and identify mismatching items. Since creating a large dataset tailored to fashion outfit analysis would be impractical, we leverage existing datasets and develop a new loss function to enhance detection accuracy. Additionally, we conduct user studies to validate our approach. Notably, our system demonstrates improved performance on existing datasets, and we demonstrate its effectiveness through live demonstrations at fashion events, showcasing users' ability to accurately identify mismatching items in their outfits using their smartphone cameras.

For centuries, science has thrived on the premise of classical descriptions. However, quantum mechanics has disrupted this tradition, paving the way to describe nonclassical phenomena. From nonclassical states and processes to the associated resource theories, every aspect of quantum physics is being explored through a fresh lens. By examining nonclassical resource theories, we gain deeper insights into the inherent qualities of quantum mechanics. Notably, these theories are propelling rapid advancements in the fields of quantum information and computation. To facilitate seamless access to this knowledge, the ACM Computing Reviews section dedicated to quantum information has established a new classification scheme: QRT. QRT encompasses diverse approaches to study nonclassical resource theories, featuring comprehensive reviews on topics such as nonclassical states and processes, quantum interactions, and their applications in communication and computation. QRT's unique hierarchy allows for seamless exploration of broad topics and nuanced subtopics, reflecting the dynamic evolution of quantum research over the past five decades. What follows is an in-depth exploration of the QRT taxonomy, accompanied by a detailed analysis of the current quantum versus classical interface, as illustrated through a detailed section breakdown.

Enhancing the scalability of private federated learning is a pressing issue. Current methods are restricted by their reliance on specific data distributions within the client population. To address this limitation, our research focuses on developing a distribution-free, private federated learning algorithm. Building on the foundation of FedBuff, which utilizes stochastic gradient descent and Bürling's bias-corrected exponential mechanism, we introduce an efficient and scalable solution. By integrating client selection based on bulk statistical characteristics and incorporating an adaptive learning rate, our approach significantly optimizes training time while maintaining robust privacy and fairness. Theoretical analysis confirms that our modified algorithm surpasses the performance of the conventional FedBuff method. Moreover, our extensive experimental evaluations demonstrate substantial reductions in training time, with minimal sacrifices in accuracy and impressive gains in usability and scalability.

Our research aims to explore an operator calculus for polynomial shift semigroups by synthesizing elements of C*-algebra semigroups and commutant theory. We develop a spectrally nested sequence of star-algebras for each polynomial shift semigroup, whose linear maps are generated by a C*-algebra that is closed under a shift operation. The closure of this sequence is a *-algebra that is, in certain instances, proven to be dense in a C*-algebra. A specific representation of the algebra is established using a commutant of the semigroup, and this representation is shown to be faithful in several cases. Additionally, our study yields a continuous, dense, and surjective homomorphism from the algebra to a C*-algebra for all polynomial degrees.

Primordial black holes with specific masses may be shedding new light on the universe's mysteries, as their existence could explain all of dark matter if present in the right quantity. Recent research using gravitational lensing data has given us a better understanding of their possible presence, giving us more information than previously had. This updated analysis uses the latest lensing dataset and a more accurate statistical method to investigate the possibility of dark matter taking the form of these black holes. The study considers various masses within a specific range and computes the production probabilities based on primordial density fluctuations' characteristics. The results provide confidence levels for dark matter composed entirely of these black holes, as well as a mixture of dark matter consisting of primordial black holes and weakly interacting massive particles. The study's predictions are more restrictive than earlier estimates for masses within a specific range, and the results for primordial black holes are further tightened when incorporating the latest planetary microlensing data. The constraints for a particular mass range are more stringently confirmed than a previous theoretical prediction based on certain astrophysical data, and the results for a different mass range align more closely with this prediction. The outcomes for dual-component dark matter consisting of these black holes and weakly interacting massive particles also show significant reductions in uncertainty, and the results for a specific mass range see a slight improvement in this allowance. The constraints for another mass range see minor reductions in this allowance, and the results for a specific mass range see minor reductions in this allowance. The outcomes for dual

The behavior of particle rafts, consisting of particles arranged in a grid with interstitial fluid, undergoes analysis through computational simulations of fluid dynamics and particle motion. As external load is applied, causing the fluid to expand and break the particle aggregate, particles re-aggregate and form a new, more compact structure. The process repeats, resulting in periodic increases and decreases in the fluid's volume. Our 2D analysis shows that the distance between particles remains stable during these cycles, and the fluid's expansion rate corresponds to the fluid's viscosity and surface tension. A theoretical model has been developed to explain the observed phenomena and predicts that the fluid's behavior is governed by a specific relationship between particle distance and fluid parameters. Our simulations accurately reproduce the theoretical model's predictions.

Gallium nitride has significant potential for high-electron-density applications, but its room-temperature hole mobility is too low, around 1 cm/Vs. By matching the lattice with ZnGeN2 and MgSiN2, we found that room-temperature hole mobility increased to 20 cm/Vs and 30 cm/Vs, respectively. Introducing a sp-d hybridized hole band resulted in higher mobilities. Gallium nitride combined with ZnGeN2 has the potential to replace SiCrN2 due to higher electron mobility and better crystalline structure. Combining it with MgSiN2 may offer comparable performance to Al0.25Ga0.75N.

Sparse policy representation through sparse gradient projection (SPGP) offers a probabilistic framework for approximating policy expectations with minimal data efficiency. This work modifies the SPGP approach to create SPGP-SARSA, a sparse expectation approximation algorithm, increasing its applicability in various reinforcement learning tasks. By integrating SPGP with off-policy Monte-Carlo target estimates, the SPGP-SARSA algorithm facilitates efficient policy evaluation without the need for sample refinement. Experimental evaluations demonstrate that SPGP-SARSA enhances the efficiency of policy evaluation in complex underwater navigation tasks, requiring a sparse navigation policy to exploit environmental sparsity. Furthermore, SPGP-SARSA exhibits a significant reduction in computational cost, along with improved robustness to noise and robustness in partial observability scenarios.

We create new isothermic surfaces by applying mappings from a group action
involved in the differential displacement of simply connected patches. To
accomplish this, we employ specific compositions of Möbius transformations and
active reals to map isothermic surfaces to a standard form called the Fundamental
Form. Conversely, using the inverse of these mappings, we can express any isothermic
surface as a composition of mappings from a base surface, which we call the Base
Surface. The use of these mappings allows for the expression of isothermic surfaces in
terms of unknown functions that can be determined using specific equations, such as
the Isothermic Constant Mean Curvature (ICMC) condition.

The article explores the potential of nonparametric kernel-based methods of regularization in PDEs compared to traditional projected methods such as the Galerkin approach.  Initially, a nonparametric formulation of the 2D Stokes equations is examined using regularization via Reproducing Kernel Hilbert Spaces.  Analysis of the resulting kernel-regularized problem indicates that the solution converges well and can be efficiently computed in the kernel space.  A comparison of the methods is made through the error of the stress tensor.  Next, the article considers nonparametric formulations of the 2D Stokes equations and the 3D Brinkman equations using the sparse approximation technique known as Gaussian Process Regression.  A comparison of kernel-based methods and the sparse approach is made through the error of the stress tensor.  The conclusions suggest that kernel-based methods provide superior convergence and can be more efficiently computed in comparison to the sparse approach, while the sparse technique offers computational advantages in comparison to the classical projected methods.
This paper introduces the $\hbar$-analogues of Dowling polynomials and establishes connections with Lagrange inequalities, Rimannian zeta polynomials, and Kostka polynomials.

Knowledge graph embeddings have been extensively researched in recent years, focusing on developing strategies to represent relationships within large knowledge graphs effectively. This study concentrates on improving temporal knowledge graph embeddings by introducing a new model called Complementary Knowledge Graph Embeddings (CKGE). CKGE addresses the limitations of current models by incorporating complementary knowledge graphs and is capable of learning distinct entity representations. Unlike existing models, CKGE is both efficient and scalable, with adaptability extending to general knowledge graphs. Experimental results demonstrate the superiority of CKGE in addressing the challenges associated with temporal knowledge graphs, while also performing competitively in general knowledge graph settings.

We examine the set of insplits and outsplits for matrices associated with weighted graphs, and we explore the connection between strong shift equivalence and these matrices. A specific subset of these matrices, which we term row-reduced positive matrices, has a lattice structure when considered as weighted graphs, and we demonstrate that this subset is closed under strong shift equivalence. Additionally, we define a binary relation ~ among row-reduced positive matrices, and we show that each class of matrices defined by this relation contains exactly one matrix that is strong shift equivalent to all other matrices within that class.

Quantum Chromodynamics predicts that the color force between two heavy quarks creates a complex potential with unknown anisotropic properties. To analyze this anisotropy, the potential's linearity and directionality are investigated by examining the structural configurations it exhibits in two-dimensional Euclidean space. To broaden the understanding of this anisotropy, the study focuses on whether the potential retains its linear and directional characteristics beyond rectangular shapes by exploring triangular configurations. The complex heavy quark potential's anisotropic properties are found to be sensitive to the angles within these triangular structures. The potential's anisotropy is also observed to depend solely on the lengths of its sides when the study is extended to quadrilateral configurations. The findings suggest that the potential's anisotropy is not an artifact of quark-antiquark corrections and that its anisotropic nature persists even when the quarks do not possess internal degrees of freedom.

This research presents OREO-LM, a semantically-interfaced large-language-model autoregressive transformer that integrates knowledge interaction and language processing on an equal footing. OREO-LM's design incorporates a Knowledge Interaction Layer that facilitates the knowledge gap filling by generating and selecting relevant knowledge chunks. This distinction sets OREO-LM apart from previous approaches that separate knowledge acquisition and language generation. By accounting for knowledge chunks during training, OREO-LM is capable of learning the meaning of individual chunks. We further develop oreo-lm-fast, a distillated version of the model that outperforms other distillated models on multiple datasets. Experimental evaluations demonstrate the superiority of OREO-LM, particularly its ability to produce answers as a collection of relevant knowledge chunks rather than a continuous sequence, thereby enhancing overall performance. Data and code are available at https://github.com/mkcao/oreo-lm.

A high dimensional expanders collection, denoted as $G_{\leq r}$, consisting of graph families where each graph has a vertex set of size $r$, would significantly benefit theoretical computer science. We nearly achieve a construction of this collection by utilizing a new type of high dimensional subspaces collection, and in the process, we make progress on a related problem by constructing a near optimal approximation scheme for a long-standing open problem known as the Cover Time Problem. Our approach involves a new type of subspaces collection, known as $\ell_2$-geometry, and in the process, we make progress on a related problem by constructing a near optimal approximation scheme for a long-standing open problem known as the Cover Time Problem. We also make progress on a related problem by constructing a near optimal approximation scheme for a long-standing open problem known as the Cover Time Problem. We nearly achieve a construction of a high dimensional expanders collection, denoted as $G_{\leq r}$, consisting of graph families where each graph has a vertex set of size $r$. We demonstrate the existence of a collection of subspaces such that for every dimension $r$, there exists a graph with a large expansion property whose vertex set corresponds to a particular type of vector space in $G_{\leq r}$.
